item.title: Android 16 KB page size, NDK 27 and a blue tint – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Android 16 KB page size: add the linker flag before you upgrade the NDK (NDK 27 and 29 tinted our photos blue)

Play's 16 KB page requirement was met with one linker flag, even on NDK 25. The NDK upgrade we made first is what put a blue tint on photo transitions.

Google Play requires apps targeting Android 15 or later to ship native libraries (.so files) aligned for 16 KB memory pages. In SugarAlbum, our app that turns photos into videos, the six arm64 libraries we build ourselves were 4 KB aligned (0x1000). In January 2026, working with an AI coding agent, we moved to NDK 26.3, added a linker flag and got them to 16 KB (0x4000). Along the way, builds made with NDK 27.0 and 29.0 put a blue cast on photo transitions.

On October 27, 2026 we rebuilt the same source with four NDK versions, and NDK 25.1, which our records called "16KB unsupported", gave 0x4000 once the linker flag was in. The upgrade was never needed. Below are the commands to measure alignment, the RELRO check that is easy to miss, and an order of checks to follow.

The three .so files rebuilt for targetSdk 36 were still 4 KB aligned

As of January 2026 SugarAlbum has 763 Java files and 32 Kotlin files, and the video and filter work runs in C/C++ libraries built with ndk-build. We raised targetSdk from 33 to 34 in July 2024 and from 34 to 36 at the end of August 2025. On August 31, 2025 we rebuilt the three arm64 libraries of the multimediaFramework module (libBeatTracker, libPixelCanvas, libPixelUtils) without telling the linker about page size, and the other three (libnative_filter, libFFmpegProcessor, libKwpFFmpegMuxer) were still the November 2022 builds. So right before the January work, all six had LOAD segments aligned to 0x1000.

Google announced on the Android Developers Blog on May 8, 2025 that starting November 1, 2025, new apps and updates targeting Android 15 or higher must support 16 KB pages. The current page size guide (updated 2026-10-16) says that starting February 1, 2027, updates without 16 KB support can't be released. Our repo notes say a Play Console warning asked for a fix "by May 2025". That date appears in neither official source, and the warning text itself isn't saved anywhere in the repo.

The January work was done with Claude Code; the commit carries its Co-Authored-By line. A work note committed alongside it records the first move: "After: NDK 27.0.12077973. Reason: the APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES flag is only supported in NDK r27 and later." The final commit used 26.3, and the work note went in still saying 27.0.

NDK 27.0 and 29.0 builds tinted photo transitions blue

The commit message has a three-line NDK table: 25.x does not support 16 KB, 26.3 works (adopted), 27.0 and 29.0 show "a blue tint bug with -O3 optimization". A work note in the same commit describes the symptom as a bluish cast during photo transitions, places it in the PixelUtils and libyuv code of the multimediaFramework module, and notes that an -O0 build looks normal. All five modules in that module's Android.mk (libYUV, libMasp, PixelCanvas, PixelUtils, BeatTracker) compile with -O3.

No automated check caught it. The only tests in the repo are the two placeholder tests Android Studio generates (ExampleUnitTest and ExampleInstrumentedTest); nothing compares colors or rendered frames. NDK 27.0 and 29.0 both built cleanly and both produced aligned libraries. The tint showed up only when someone ran the app and watched a transition.

The work note names the cause as "a Clang -O3 optimization bug". The only evidence on record is that -O0 looks fine. The bundled compilers are clang 17.0.2 in NDK 26.3, 18.0.1 in 27.0 and 21.0.0 in 29.0, so the tint lines up with clang 18 and later. A clean -O0 build is also what you'd see if our own code had undefined behavior that the newer optimizer treats differently, and nobody narrowed it down to a function.

The same commit tidied the libyuv NEON lines in Android.mk, so we checked that too. libPixelUtils.so exports 198 symbols with NEON in the name both before and after the commit. The NEON code was already in the old build, so it isn't the variable.

NDK 26.3 ignores APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES

The final commit sets alignment in three places: android.ndk.maxPageSize=16384 in gradle.properties, APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES := true in three Application.mk files, and LOCAL_LDFLAGS += -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 in six Android.mk modules. To see which one did the work, we searched each NDK's build/core for the flag name. It isn't in 25.1 or 26.3; it's only in build-binary.mk of 27.0 and 29.0. In 27.0, a true value adds max-page-size=16384 to the link. In 29.0, 16 KB is the default and a false value sets it back to 4096.

Then we rebuilt the libnative_filter source from the January commit (two C files) with each NDK and read the LOAD alignment with llvm-readelf -lW on 2026-10-27.

NDKLinker flag in Android.mkarm64-v8a LOAD alignment
25.1.8937393no0x1000
25.1.8937393yes0x4000
26.3.11579264no (Application.mk flag only)0x1000
26.3.11579264yes (as committed)0x4000
27.0.12077973no (Application.mk flag only)0x4000
29.0.14206865no0x4000

Under 26.3 the 16 KB alignment came from the Android.mk linker flag; the Application.mk line did nothing. The same flag gave 0x4000 under 25.1. The commit's "NDK 25.x: 16KB unsupported" was never tested with the flag in place, and it follows from the first assumption that the feature needs r27. The official guide's "Android NDK r27 and lower" section also gets 16 KB alignment from the max-page-size and common-page-size linker flags and never mentions APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES.

The six prebuilt FFmpeg libraries pass the LOAD check and fail the RELRO formula

The work note left six prebuilt FFmpeg libraries (libavcodec-56, libavfilter-5, libavformat-56, libavutil-54, libswresample-1, libswscale-3) marked as needing a separate 16 KB rebuild. Their LOAD segments were already aligned to 0x10000 (64 KB) before the commit. 64 KB is a multiple of 16 KB, so they pass the guide's rule that no LOAD segment may be below 2**14.

The guide has a second check. (VirtAddr + MemSiz) of the GNU_RELRO segment should divide evenly by 0x4000. If it doesn't, and RELRO shares a LOAD segment with writable data that follows it (.data, .bss), the app can crash at runtime with a segmentation fault. A LOAD segment holding only RELRO data, followed by a writable LOAD that starts on a separate 16 KB page, is a case where the formula doesn't apply; the guide's example of that layout is still 16 KB compliant. We ran all twelve arm64 libraries from the January commit through that formula.

LibraryRELRO end % 0x4000Result
libnative_filter, libBeatTracker, libFFmpegProcessor, libKwpFFmpegMuxer0x0pass
libPixelCanvas, libPixelUtils0x1000formula doesn't apply (RELRO-only LOAD)
six prebuilt FFmpeg libraries0x1000 to 0x3000RELRO shares a LOAD with .data/.bss

In libavcodec-56, the writable LOAD segment is 0x257f00 bytes in memory and only its first 0xfbf8 bytes are RELRO, which is the shape the guide uses as its crash example. The commit added only max-page-size; the guide's examples also pass common-page-size=16384. Our six self-built libraries passed without it. The repo has FFmpeg's source and build scripts, but nothing records which flags produced the .so files it ships. The work note says -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 was added to both build scripts; in this commit the scripts were only moved, and their linker flag variable (ADDI_LDFLAGS) doesn't have that flag.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Keeping NDK 25.1 and adding the linker flag would have worked

There were three ways to go in January. We pinned NDK 26.3 and wrote "do not use NDK 27 or later" into the notes.

  • Stay on NDK 25.1 and add the linker flag. The table above says alignment would have been fine, and since the records show no tint on 25.1 and the compiler would have stayed the same, there was no reason to expect a color regression. It was ruled out by the "25 unsupported" call.
  • Use NDK 27 or 29 and lower -O3 only in multimediaFramework. -O0 is recorded as looking fine, but nobody measured how much slower video processing gets.
  • Find and fix the function that shifts the color. There's no record of an attempt.

Don't upgrade the NDK first. Put the linker flag into the NDK you already use and check the alignment with readelf. If you have another reason to move to a newer NDK, do it as a separate change and compare rendered output against the previous build.

CMake builds and NDK r28 or later need a different procedure

This is an ndk-build project (Android.mk, Application.mk). With CMake, the guide puts the flags in target_link_options, and the Android.mk line is irrelevant. NDK r28 and later align to 16 KB by default, so the flag isn't needed at all; our 29.0 build gave 0x4000 on arm64 with no flag.

There's no basis for saying NDK 27 will do the same to other code. We didn't check 32-bit (armeabi-v7a) libraries; the guide's requirement covers 64-bit devices.

Checking with readelf twice and the same set of photos

  1. For each arm64-v8a .so that ships in the APK or AAB, read the LOAD alignment. The last column must be 0x4000 or larger.
    llvm-readelf -lW libfoo.so | grep -E "LOAD|GNU_RELRO"
  2. If there's a GNU_RELRO line, add VirtAddr and MemSiz and take the remainder mod 0x4000. If it isn't zero, check whether the LOAD segment holding RELRO also holds .data/.bss (its MemSiz is much larger than RELRO's).
  3. Before changing the NDK, add both flags from the guide to Android.mk in your current NDK and repeat step 1.
    LOCAL_LDFLAGS += -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 -Wl,-z,common-page-size=16384
  4. APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES is read only by NDK r27 and later. On r26 or older, that line alone does nothing.
  5. Delete the .so files in jniLibs and rebuild every time you change the NDK or the flags. Our notes record that Android Studio's Clean Project doesn't remove jniLibs, so the build script deletes them first.
  6. Export a video from the same photos with the old build and the new one, and watch the transitions side by side.
  7. If you ship uncompressed .so files, confirm Android Gradle Plugin 8.5.1 or later and run zipalign -v -c -P 16 4 app.apk. SugarAlbum uses AGP 8.12.0.

Another Play Console warning we traced is in Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized. The culprit was a keep rule for an SDK we never used. The app itself is on the SugarAlbum page.

Not done yet: a 16 KB emulator run and a per-module -O3 check

Video export has to run end to end on a 16 KB page emulator image to see whether the FFmpeg libraries crash on RELRO. If they do, FFmpeg needs a rebuild with common-page-size=16384. We still don't know which module the tint comes from; one way to narrow it down is to take the five multimediaFramework modules off -O3 one at a time. The NDK 27.0 in the work note should be corrected to 26.3.

Questions, consulting or collaboration

Email us with a question about this note, consulting on app development or on adopting AI agents such as Claude Code, or a collaboration idea.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com · Subscribe via RSS

FAQ

Do I need NDK r27 or later to support 16 KB pages?

Not for the alignment itself. With -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 in Android.mk, NDK 25.1 rebuilt libnative_filter.so (arm64) with 0x4000 LOAD alignment (measured 2026-10-27). r27 is only needed for the one-line APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES approach.

How do I check whether a .so is 16 KB aligned?

Run llvm-readelf -lW or llvm-objdump -p and confirm every LOAD segment is aligned to 0x4000 (2**14) or more. If GNU_RELRO shares a LOAD segment with writable data, also check that (VirtAddr + MemSiz) % 0x4000 is zero.

Can I keep a prebuilt .so that is 64 KB aligned?

It passes the LOAD alignment check. SugarAlbum's six FFmpeg libraries are 0x10000 and pass that check, but their RELRO remainders are 0x1000 to 0x3000.

Checked 2026-10-27. SugarAlbum git history and work notes, .so alignment rechecked with llvm-readelf, and the official Android Developers documentation.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • "6.7" < "6.11" is false: comparing Remote Config versions as strings froze content updates
  • Fitting a JPEG under a file size limit: quality binary search, a predicted long edge, and a final check against the original
  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException
  • The first LLM feature in a spell-check app: cost, model evaluation and daily caps for "Why is this wrong?"
  • 4.5:1 contrast in the site build: the dark hover pair that failed for 7 of 11 apps
  • Rapid taps and an unlocked Retry button: a 600 ms result-card lock, and the 28 crashes a stress run found next

item.title: AI app design review: 3 agent designs, 3 judges – SugarMount
item.description:
AX Notes · How-to

Three agent designs, three judges: the market judge alone would have picked the one that crashed on every KakaoTalk file

Use at least three design judges with different viewpoints and pick the winner by total score. With only our market-veteran judge, the winning design would have crashed on every file opened from KakaoTalk.

Building the SugarDoc HWP viewer 1/8

If you have AI agents write competing designs and other agents grade them, who sits on the panel decides the winner. Before writing any code for SugarDoc, our Android viewer for HWP, HWPX and PDF documents, we had three designs that differed only in priority scored by three judges with different viewpoints. The market judge's favorite would have crashed every time someone opened a document received in KakaoTalk; the Android-engineer and policy judges caught it. All of this happened in 59 minutes before any code existed, and the crashing entry point never reached the repository.

59 minutes before any code: research, refutation, three designs, judging, critique

HWP and HWPX are the file formats of Hangul, the word processor Korean schools and government offices use, and many people receive these files through KakaoTalk, Korea's dominant messenger. On the evening of October 4 we had market research and an engine spike for a viewer (the engine numbers are in Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents) and zero lines of code. At 21:34 KST the main session wrote one Claude Code Workflow script and started it.

The script has five stages. Twelve agents research twelve areas separately: competitors, the HWP engine, the PDF engine, intents and entry, the received-documents inbox, monetization, UX, the codebase, store search, quality, security and scope. Two reviewers per area then try to break each report. Any finding that at least one of the 24 verification reports marked refuted was deleted before design; there were 16. From what remained, three design agents wrote designs that differ only in priority, three judges scored them, and one critic checked the final plan made from the winner plus ideas grafted from the others. A last agent was assigned five documents: analysis, PRD, screen contract, architecture and implementation plan.

In all, 45 agents used 8.8 million tokens in 59 minutes. Research ran from minute 0 to 16 and verification, starting on each area as soon as its research finished, from 7 to 26. The three designs took 6 minutes, judging two and a half, and synthesis, critique and document writing 25.

The three design prompts differed by one sentence

Every agent got the same shared context: the repository layout (minSdk 29, targetSdk 36), where the earlier research lived, the goal, a rule to tag each claim as verified, inferred or unverified, and a ban on editing files, installing packages, committing or touching devices. Each stage returned JSON against a fixed schema.

StageGist of the instructionOutput
VerifyOne reviewer always fact-checks: if you cannot reproduce the evidence yourself, default to refuted or uncertain. The other takes an area lens: market, feasibility, Android platform, policy or userconfirmed/refuted/uncertain per finding, keep/change/drop per recommendation, what is missing
DesignUse only the verified dossier, answer the reviewers' pushback, never build the design on an uncertain finding without a validation step; one priority sentence (speed, quality or growth)scope, architecture, screens, quality gates, milestones with day estimates, risks
JudgeOne persona. Score 0 to 10 on win potential, feasibility, reliability, revenue and policy safety. Be harsh, find fatal flaws, pick a winner, list ideas to graftscores, winner, grafts, fatal flaws
CritiqueDoes every release feature have a milestone and a test, every risk a mitigation or validation task? Are the ad rules enforced by tests? Are estimates realistic for one developer plus Claude? Are human-only tasks listed?each gap rated blocker, major or minor, with a fix

The three priority sentences: speed, "reach the internal track in two to three weeks, inside the October demand window, without giving up never-fails-to-open and no ads on documents"; quality, "open everything correctly and fast on low-end phones, with the strongest regression and crash guardrails"; growth, "maximize installs, return visits and revenue within the trust rules". The judges were a Korean mobile market veteran who had shipped top-10 utility apps, a staff Android engineer responsible for crash-free rate and APK size on low-end Samsung phones, and a Google Play and AdMob policy and privacy reviewer. The script picked the winner by the sum of the three judges' totals. A majority vote would also have chosen quality, the pick of judges 2 and 3; with only the speed design on the table, the NoDisplay entry would have gone straight to implementation.

The speed design's entry point: async copy in a NoDisplay activity

The speed design planned nine milestones totalling 20.5 days. All document intents went to one EntryActivity with Theme.NoDisplay. On Dispatchers.IO it would take the URI, sniff the format from the first 64 KB, copy the file into app storage while hashing it with SHA-256, start the reader and finish, showing progress and a cancel button after one second.

A NoDisplay activity has to call finish() before onResume() completes. For apps targeting API 23 or higher on Android 6.0 or later, one that does not crashes with IllegalStateException and the message "did not call finish() prior to onResume() completing". A CommonsWare blog post flagged it in November 2015 and noted that activities doing their work in onCreate() and finishing right there seem to be fine. Our app targets API 36, and an async copy finishes after onResume(), so as designed, every "open with" from KakaoTalk would have crashed the app.

At design time there was no code to run. Written as designed, it would compile; it shows up only in a test that runs the activity lifecycle, such as Robolectric, or when a device opens a file through a VIEW intent. Judge 2 called it easy to fix but fatal if built as written. Judge 3 said to switch to Theme.Translucent.NoTitleBar.

The final plan has the reader activity take VIEW intents directly, and a Translucent SendEntryActivity hand shared files on and finish inside onCreate(). The architecture document lists the NoDisplay entry as a rejected option, and the PRD acceptance criteria include "zero Theme.NoDisplay activities".

Judge 1 picked the design with the crash

JudgespeedqualitygrowthPick
1 market veteran343332speed
2 Android engineer293534quality
3 policy and privacy reviewer323632quality
Total9510498quality

Judge 1 listed ten fatal flaws, none of them NoDisplay. The three judges gave speed 8, 7 and 8 for win potential. Quality got 9 for reliability from all three, but its milestones added up to 44 days, and all three said it would miss the October demand window. Growth (39 days) contradicted itself: one quality gate required switching to a preview within 6 seconds while its state machine showed a notice at 8 seconds and terminated at 30.

Judge 3 also caught that the app lock in the speed and growth designs used BIOMETRIC_STRONG|DEVICE_CREDENTIAL, which API 28 and 29 do not support. With minSdk 29, that paid feature would not have worked on Android 10 phones. The judges' 25 fatal flaws were merged into nine rows in the analysis document, each with its fix.

23 gaps in the merged plan: a schedule that did not add up and a gate that could not run

The synthesis agent started from the quality design, grafted in the speed design's scope cuts and parallel work, and fixed every fatal flaw. The critic's checklist found 2 blockers, 10 major and 11 minor gaps in the result.

Blocker 1 was arithmetic: the milestones on the critical path summed to 23 working days, so even with no weekends the internal-track date was already missed. Blocker 2 was a release gate that could not run. It required a shell script to pass on a Firebase Test Lab device, and Test Lab gives you no adb shell. The gate was split in two, and the first build milestone (M1) got a spike for instrumented tests on a release build.

One major gap concerned password-protected files. For a fast first screen, the plan showed the preview image stored inside the HWP file before rendering, and a research-stage experiment had found that image in encrypted documents too, so the first page would show before the password. It became one functional requirement and one architecture section. The analysis document has a table mapping each of the 23 gaps to where it was fixed.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The NoDisplay entry never reached git, and the ban test closed two bypasses

Early on October 5 the first implementation workflow (M1 and M2) added a NoDisplay ban to an architecture test. A review agent in the same workflow found two ways around it: the <application> theme, which activities inherit, and a style item android:windowNoDisplay=true. The test, which never launches an activity, now reads every themed element in the manifest plus style parents and that item, and each bypass was planted once to confirm the test fails.

Only one commit in the history contains the word NoDisplay: the October 8 internal test build, which brought in the ban test and the design documents. On October 9 the owner sent HWPX, HWP5, PDF and HWP3 files from another KakaoTalk account to a Galaxy S23 and all four opened.

The NoDisplay entry was first proposed by a refuting reviewer

The intents research report never mentioned NoDisplay. The entry came from the fact-checking reviewer of that report, as its suggested replacement: "VIEW and SEND are received by a very light trampoline (Theme.NoDisplay, excludeFromRecents, noHistory)", with the trampoline starting the 64 KB sniff and the copy. That text went into the dossier and the speed design followed it. The quality and growth designs did not use the NoDisplay theme.

Judge 3 tagged the NoDisplay flaw "[verified, Android 6.0 behavior change]", but that agent made one tool call, the one that submitted its result, so the tag was added without opening anything. The claim was right; we confirmed it against the CommonsWare post while writing this. The three design agents and judge 3 worked only from the dossier pasted into the prompt; judges 1 and 2 looked at the git history and spike files once or twice.

The schedule estimate was wrong in the other direction. The analysis said the original November 3 production date could not be met and set the internal track for November 2, production for November 9 and November 13 to 16 as the worst case. The internal track came on October 8 and the public release on October 10. Some milestone exit criteria, such as purchase restore, the app lock on API 29 and TalkBack checks on a device, were still open at release. We had told the critic to judge estimates for one developer plus Claude; the build then ran as separate workflows, one or two milestones each.

The document-writing agent was assigned five files and wrote four. The agent's permission settings blocked it from writing the analysis report as a file; it did not work around the block and returned the text in its answer, which the main session saved; the workflow record lists all 45 agents as done.

How to run it: the script skeleton and the order

A trimmed skeleton of the real script: prompt text removed, and helper names such as dropRefuted, argmax and sumTotals are illustrative (the original does this inline). agent, parallel and pipeline come from Claude Code Workflow scripts.

const verified = await pipeline(AREAS,
  a => agent(CTX + a.task, { schema: REPORT }),
  (r, a) => parallel(['fact-check', a.lens].map(l => () =>
    agent(CTX + LENS[l] + JSON.stringify(r), { schema: VERDICT }))))
const dossier = dropRefuted(verified)          // 16 findings removed
const designs = await parallel(ANGLES.map(an => () =>
  agent(CTX + an.priority + dossier, { schema: DESIGN })))
const judged = await parallel(JUDGES.map(j => () =>
  agent(CTX + j + designs + dossier, { schema: SCORE })))
const winner = argmax(sumTotals(judged))       // sum, not one judge
const final = await agent(CTX + winner + designs + judged + dossier, { schema: DESIGN })
const gaps = await agent(CTX + CHECKLIST + final + dossier, { schema: CRIT })
  1. Give every research area one fact-checking reviewer and one reviewer with an area lens, and drop refuted findings before design.
  2. Have every design use the same dossier and the same schema, changing only the priority sentence. Put day estimates in the schema so schedules can be compared.
  3. Use three judges from different angles, such as market, engineering and policy, and decide by the total. Ask for fatal flaws and graft ideas separately.
  4. Run a checklist critique on the final plan, and keep a table of where each gap was fixed.
  5. Pin each fatal flaw with a rule test, such as an architecture test that parses the manifest and styles, and remove the guard once to see the test fail.
  6. Keep checks only a person can do, like opening files on a real phone, on a separate list and close them there.

Review after the code exists is a different process; we ran one where every finding faces three refuting agents, described in AI code review findings: fix only what survives refutation.

When 8.8 million tokens and an hour are wasted

Verification used the most tokens, 2.95 million. The nine design, judge and synthesis agents made 21 tool calls between them and used 3.84 million tokens, because each prompt carried the whole dossier as JSON. We did not record a dollar cost.

If the design has nothing to argue about, say one more screen or a feature whose API is already chosen, this is too much. Here a new app, two rendering engines, the entry path, monetization and Play policy were all in play at once. Every agent was the same model reading the same dossier, so a flaw they all miss stays missed, and the scores are not calibrated: the same speed design got anywhere from 29 to 34.

What to check next

As of the October 9 record, opening files received through Naver Mail (a major Korean email service) and Gmail had not been tested on a device.

Questions, consulting or collaboration

Email us with a question about this note, consulting on app development or on adopting AI agents such as Claude Code, or a collaboration idea.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com · Subscribe via RSS

Building the SugarDoc HWP viewer: all 8 parts

  1. Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents

FAQ

Is one judge enough?

Not in this run. With only the market-veteran judge, the speed design with the NoDisplay crash would have won with 34 points. The Android engineer and policy reviewer personas caught the crash.

Why does a Theme.NoDisplay activity crash?

For apps targeting API 23 or higher on Android 6.0 or later, a NoDisplay activity that has not called finish() by the end of onResume() throws IllegalStateException. If the work is asynchronous, use a Translucent theme or receive the intent in a real screen.

Sources: git history and design documents in the SugarDoc repository and the Claude Code session logs (workflow script, per-agent transcripts), as of October 26, 2026.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • We set interstitial frequency from device timelines, and tutorials don't count
  • We built three photo apps before checking the market: this year's new apps had a median of 1,166 installs

item.title: java.time on Android 7: Call requires API level 26 – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

A launch crash only on Android 7: one java.time call in a shared module and a NewApi lint gate

If a minSdk 24 app closes at launch only on Android 7, suspect an API 26 class such as java.time. One such line in a shared module crashed two of our games for two weeks.

Our arrow puzzle game (minSdk 24) closed on Android 7 before drawing its first screen: GA4 recorded app_exception on first launch and no screen views. Our block puzzle shares the same module and runs the same path. A sub-agent we dispatched at 08:50 on October 17, 2026 (KST) to analyze drop-off in the arrow game reported this at 08:56. The cause was one line in the ad module both games share. It called java.time, which exists only from API 26, in apps with minSdk 24, and it runs on every launch. The line had been in the code since a commit on October 3. We submitted fixed versions of both games at 09:29 the same day, and at 15:05 we watched the release builds start on an Android 7.0 emulator that had booted at 15:04.

Sources: the game repository's git history, build files and test code, the work log from the day of the fix and the GA4 drop-off analysis (code rechecked on October 25, 2026).

The line every launch runs: from Ads.start to java.time

Both apps, Block Turn and Arrow Knots, call Ads.start() from the shared core-platform module in their first Activity's onCreate. On the first start of the process, that calls onLaunch() on Pacer, the class that spaces out ads, and rollDay() inside it works out the local day number so daily ad caps reset at midnight. This was the default for that calculation:

private val day: (Long) -> Long = { java.time.Instant.ofEpochMilli(it).atZone(java.time.ZoneId.systemDefault()).toLocalDate().toEpochDay() },

Android ships java.time from Android 8.0 (API 26). Both apps and core-platform have minSdk 24, and nothing in the repository turns on core library desugaring. An Android 7 phone does not have the class, so the app dies before it draws anything. This is the lint output from later, when we put the old line back to test the gate:

Pacer.kt:68: Error: Call requires API level 26, or core library desugaring (current min is 24): java.time.Instant#atZone [NewApi]

The sub-agent found the crash in the arrow game's data and added in the same report that Block Turn uses the same core-platform and would crash the same way.

For two weeks, no check ran that line on Android 7

The October 3 commit that added the line was co-written with the agent, and its message ends with a verification note: "Verified on S21 … release (R8, test ads) monkey 3x1500 0 fatals." That is a release build, three monkey runs of 1,500 events and zero fatal errors, on an S21 running Android 15; minSdk 24 was never exercised by that check.

Our other phone, a Galaxy S20, runs Android 13, and the emulator images on the PC were API 30, 33, 34 and 35.

The unit tests never executed the line. Pacer was written as a pure class so every ad rule could be tested without Android, and all 13 tests build it through one helper, Pacer(rules, state, now = { t }, day = { today }). Injecting the clock and the day made the rules easy to test, and the injected spot was exactly the default that crashed. The JVM has java.time, so the line would have passed there anyway.

The release build never ran lint on the shared module. On October 17, :core-platform:lintDebug flagged NewApi on the old line, but the lint that runs automatically with a release build belonged to the app modules.

The next day, two other files avoided java.time

Early on October 4, the commit that added Block Turn formats a date string with SimpleDateFormat and comments "java.time needs API 26". That night, the daily puzzle commit for Arrow Knots computes dates with Howard Hinnant's civil algorithms, commented "so the app needs no java.time (minSdk 24, no desugaring)". The line added to the shared module the day before stayed as it was.

On October 17, rg -n "java\.time" --type kotlin across seven modules found exactly one java.time call in running code: that line in Pacer.

The fix uses only java.util.TimeZone:

fun localEpochDay(ms: Long, zone: java.util.TimeZone = java.util.TimeZone.getDefault()): Long =
    Math.floorDiv(ms + zone.getOffset(ms), 86_400_000L)

This time the default itself is under test. LocalEpochDayTest walks seven time zones, including Asia/Seoul, America/New_York, Pacific/Kiritimati and America/Adak, for 400 days from December 31, 2025 in 37-minute steps, and compares each result with java.time on the JVM. Steps of 37 minutes cross every midnight and every daylight saving switch.

Lint settings in the app module did not stop the shared module

The first attempt at a guard was wrong. The agent added lint { checkDependencies = true; fatal += "NewApi" } to both apps' build.gradle.kts, expecting that checking dependencies and raising NewApi to fatal would block the release build. It put the old java.time line back for a moment and ran :app-block:lintVitalRelease. The result was BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 29s.

The second attempt made the shared module run its own lint before every release build:

// core-platform/build.gradle.kts
lint {
    checkOnly += "NewApi"
    abortOnError = true
}
// app-block/build.gradle.kts, app-arrows/build.gradle.kts
tasks.matching { it.name == "preReleaseBuild" }.configureEach { dependsOn(":core-platform:lintRelease") }

At 09:04, with the old line back in, the release build stopped with the NewApi error above, BUILD FAILED in 28s and exit code 1. With the fixed line, :core-platform:lintRelease exited 0. The build file comment records the reason as "lintVitalRelease does not look into library modules", and the first setting was removed.

Before shipping we also looked inside the release dex. Unzipping it and searching for Ljava/time/ still finds Instant, ZonedDateTime and more. Running dexdump to find the calling classes and matching them against R8's mapping.txt showed a Compose API-version helper and Firebase classes; our own code had none. A follow-up commit then took Arrow Knots from 1.2.1 (versionCode 6) to 1.2.2 and Block Turn from 1.1.2 (versionCode 5) to 1.1.3. That commit also carries unrelated changes such as a new order for the first puzzles, so it touches 19 files with 241 added lines.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The Android 7 emulator booted five minutes after the download started

On the morning of October 17 the agent noted the S20 and S21 could not answer the question and queried the Firebase Test Lab device list. The only models supporting API 26 or lower were four virtual devices, and the lowest level any of them offered was 26.

In its afternoon report the agent recommended waiting: watch a few days of Crashlytics data from real users on the new versions for Android 7 crashes. Downloading an Android 7 image (about 1 GB) for an emulator was its second option, pending approval. It also pointed out that buying a Galaxy S23 would not help, since it runs Android 14 or later. The operator approved the download (this setup asks before installing anything). It started at 14:59, and the Android 7.0 AVD booted at 15:04.

By then a 12:44 commit had produced the next versions, Block Turn 1.1.4 and Arrow Knots 1.2.3, and both were public by the 14:51 report. We installed release APKs of those versions and started them with am start -W: both returned Status: ok, with an empty crash buffer. The analysis document from October 18 records:

Android 7.0 emulator, release (R8) buildBlock Turn 1.1.4Arrow Knots 1.2.3
Crash on launchNone (0 FATAL)None (0 FATAL)
Time to first screen2.2 s1.3 s
Monkey (seeds 7, 21, 99; 600 to 800 events)0 crashes, 0 ANRs0 crashes, 0 ANRs

On Block Turn's first pass with seed 7, the emulator's system_server died with DeadSystemException. Two more runs with the same seed did not repeat it, and there was no crash log for our process. (The grey bar with the app name that appeared during monkey runs was Android 7's split-screen caption.)

We now keep this emulator for minSdk 24 regression checks. If your minSdk is 24, do not call a release verified until the release build has started on an API 24 emulator.

The gate covers one module and one lint check

Another shared module would need the same dependsOn line in every app. Because checkOnly turns on NewApi alone, no other lint issue stops the build at this step. The full order of our release checks is in AI-built Android app release checklist: R8 and real devices.

The emulator ran a Google APIs x86_64 image, and the builds checked used test ad IDs.

The evidence for the cause is the GA4 events, the call path in the code, and the lint result. The exception name, NoClassDefFoundError, comes from the code comment and the analysis; we did not see it in a local stack trace.

Projects that use desugaring are in a different position: the lint message itself offers "or core library desugaring". In this repository two other files were already written without it, and the code to fix was one line. There is no record of comparing the two approaches.

From two rg commands to an API 24 AVD

  1. Run rg -n "java\.time" --type kotlin and rg -n "desugar|minSdk" */build.gradle.kts over every module to find calls in running code and see whether desugaring is on.
  2. For each shared (library) module, run ./gradlew :module:lintDebug and look for NewApi in the lint-results XML.
  3. Add lint { checkOnly += "NewApi"; abortOnError = true } to the shared module, and make each app's preReleaseBuild depend on that module's lintRelease.
  4. Put the bad line back and confirm the release build fails, then restore it and confirm it passes. If the old line passes, the setting is not a gate.
  5. For classes that take an injected clock or day function, test the default too: use java.time on the JVM as the expected value and sweep several time zones and daylight saving changes.
  6. Download the image with sdkmanager "system-images;android-24;google_apis;x86_64", create an AVD, install the release APK, and run am start -W, logcat -b crash and a three-seed monkey test.
  7. For any Ljava/time/ reference left in the release dex, find the owning class through mapping.txt. Library code that branches on API level can stay.

What is left

No phone with a manufacturer's Android 7 build has run the apps yet. There is also no record of starting a pre-fix build on this emulator, so reproducing the crash and its exception name there is the next check. We have not counted affected users and will not put a number here until we have.

Questions, consulting or collaboration

Email us with a question about this note, consulting on app development or on adopting AI agents such as Claude Code, or a collaboration idea.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com · Subscribe via RSS

Frequently asked questions

Why does java.time crash a minSdk 24 app only on Android 7?

Android includes the java.time classes only from Android 8.0 (API 26). Without core library desugaring, an Android 7 device does not have them, and the app dies when it reaches the call. Android 8+ devices and JVM unit tests never show the problem.

Why doesn't a release build catch NewApi errors in a library module?

In this project, the lintVitalRelease task that runs with a release build did not look into the library module. Even with checkDependencies = true and fatal += "NewApi" in the app, the old code passed. Making the app's preReleaseBuild depend on the library's lintRelease is what stopped it.

How can I test on Android 7 without an Android 7 phone?

Create an emulator from the API 24 system image and start your release build on it. The Firebase Test Lab list we checked on October 17, 2026 had no API 24 or 25 devices. The emulator still lacks a manufacturer's system build.

item.title: AI commit provenance: what Co-Authored-By misses – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Commits without a Co-Authored-By trailer: the agent made 26 of the 29 we could check

Do not report a Co-Authored-By count as the share of AI-written code. Of 29 commits without the trailer that we could check against session logs, the agent made 26.

AI coding agents such as Claude Code add a Co-Authored-By: Claude line (a trailer) to the end of their commit messages, so it is tempting to count trailer commits and call that the AI's share. We checked the trailer-less commits in the repository of our Korean spell-checker app against the agent's own command history: 26 of 29 were merges (25) and a revert (1) that the agent ran.

When an agent runs git merge or git revert with git's default message, the trailer is simply not there. A trailer count is a lower bound on the agent's work, and it only becomes accurate once the agent's instructions say to add the trailer to merges and reverts too.

Matched against session logs, 26 of 29 were agent commands

A missing trailer says nothing about who made the commit. So we went through the Claude Code session logs (JSONL files) and collected every command the agent ran that contained git commit, merge, revert, stash, tag and the like and pointed at this repository. A commit counted as "agent command found" when such a command ran between ten minutes before and 30 seconds after the commit time.

The logs cover the evening of September 13, 2026 to October 24, a window with 282 commits. All 253 commits with a trailer matched an agent command, so the method finds the agent's commits without missing any.

In this window 89.7% of commits carry the trailer, but 279 commits, 98.9%, match a git command the agent ran. The gaps came in three shapes:

  • git revert --no-edit: it reverted a trailer commit made 28 minutes earlier, and the revert itself has no trailer.
  • git merge --no-edit main: git's default merge message has no trailer.
  • git merge -m "…": the agent wrote the message itself and still left the trailer line out.

The three merges in the same period that do carry a trailer are all cases where the agent put the trailer into its -m message. The remaining three (a version commit and two release merges) have no matching command in the logs, so we left them undecided.

Matching on time alone could produce coincidences, so we shifted every commit time by three hours in each direction and ran the same match. Only 17 and 15 of the 253 trailer commits matched (6 to 7%), and 0 and 1 of the 29 without a trailer.

Over a longer window, most of the 89 gaps are merges and stash

Without session logs, all you can sort by is subject line and date. Since August 1, 2025, 345 of the spell checker's 434 commits (79.5%) carry the trailer. The 89 without it break down as below. We matched Co-Authored-By: Claude at the start of a message line, and git's own trailer parser gave the same count.

GroupCountHow we sorted it
git-flow release merges37Subject Merge branch 'release/…', 'hotfix/…' or Merge tag …
Feature, sync and PR merges139 feature branches, 3 syncs between develop and main, 1 pull request
Stash entries2On main: … and its index on main: …
Before the first trailer7August 3 to the morning of August 7, 2025
Other single-parent commits3024 code, 5 data or config, 1 revert

The two stash entries are not commits anyone meant to count. git log --all follows refs/stash as well, so the newest stash and its index commit show up. Put --exclude=refs/stash before --all and the share becomes 345 of 432 (79.9%). Drop merges and start the window at the first trailer, and it rises to 342 of 372 single-parent commits (91.9%).

The five data or config commits were image and PSD files, two-line version bumps, a .gitignore cleanup and quiz data. All 24 code commits fall between August 9 and September 13, 2025; one of them is the operator reverting source the AI had changed wrongly (the story is in our note on 701 commit messages).

In three other repositories the gaps are mostly merges too

RepositoryFirst commitCommitsTrailerShareNo trailer (merges)
Spell checker, all history2020-12-1672534547.6%380 (205)
Spell checker, since Aug 202543434579.5%89 (51)
Utilities app2026-09-20878092.0%7 (6)
Puzzle game2026-09-3017016094.1%10 (10)
P2P chat app2025-08-2110310299.0%1 (0)

Repositories built with the agent from day one look the same. All 10 trailer-less commits in the puzzle game are merges, and all 10 line up with an agent git command in the session logs. In the utilities app, 5 of the 6 merges are the agent running git merge --no-edit on branches from the worktree folders Claude Code created for its subagents. The one single-parent commit there is the agent's own git commit -m without the trailer line. The single gap in the P2P chat app is its root commit, "first commit".

We looked for other signals and found none we could use. Every commit had the same author account. Two pull requests labeled codex were closed without merging, so their commits never appear in git log --all. Branch names survive a merge only in the merge commit's subject.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Counting your own repository

These run as-is in Git Bash or a macOS or Linux shell. Change the cutoff and the trailer text to match your repository.

U=2026-10-25T00:00:00; S=2025-08-01T00:00:00
P='^Co-Authored-By: Claude'
# 1. total and trailer commits (stash excluded)
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --since=$S --until=$U --format=%h | wc -l
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --since=$S --until=$U -i -E --grep="$P" --format=%h | wc -l
# 2. commits without the trailer, merges among them
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --since=$S --until=$U -i -E --grep="$P" --invert-grep --format=%h | wc -l
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --merges --since=$S --until=$U -i -E --grep="$P" --invert-grep --format='%h %s'
# 3. cross-check with git's trailer parser
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --until=$U --format='%(trailers:key=Co-authored-by,valueonly)' | grep -ci claude
# 4. single-parent commits without the trailer, with size
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --no-merges --since=$S --until=$U -i -E --grep="$P" --invert-grep --stat --format='%h %ad %s' --date=short
  1. Fix the cutoff with --until. In a repository that gets commits every day, the totals change within hours; this one got five new commits on the morning of October 25 alone.
  2. Find the date of the first trailer (first line with --reverse) and start the window there.
  3. Sort the commits without a trailer into merges, stash entries, data or config, and code.
  4. If you have session logs, match commit times against the times of the agent's git commands, and shift the times by a few hours to measure how often they match by chance.

To close the gaps going forward, tell the agent in its instruction file (CLAUDE.md for Claude Code) to add the trailer to merges and reverts as well. For a merge, put it on the last line of git merge --no-ff -m "message"; for a revert, run git revert --no-commit <commit> and then git commit -m with the trailer. After resolving a merge conflict, add the same line to the git commit -m that concludes it.

Periods without session logs and squash merges cannot be settled

In the spell checker, the 51 trailer-less commits made after the first trailer but before the session logs start (23 merges, 28 single-parent commits) stay undecided. The 24 code commits among them added 5,749 lines of Kotlin and Java, while the 39 trailer commits of the same weeks added 14,762. Why a trailer count is not a share of code lines is covered in the 701-commit note.

With squash merges, one pull request becomes one commit, and the trailer depends on the tool of whoever presses the merge button. In repositories with many contributors, each person's commit habits make the ratio harder to read. Tools that keep no session logs, or setups that delete them, rule out the cross-check entirely. In a GitLab survey of 1,528 developers and technology buyers in six countries, released on June 23, 2026, 43% said they cannot reliably tell AI-generated code from human-written code (GitLab press release).

What we will check next

When we checked on October 25, the spell checker's instruction file said nothing about trailers. Once a rule for merges and reverts is written down, the trailer-less merges have to be counted again to see whether it worked.

Questions, consulting or collaboration

Email us with a question about this note, consulting on app development or on adopting AI agents such as Claude Code, or a collaboration idea.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com · Subscribe via RSS

Frequently asked questions

Does a commit without a Co-Authored-By trailer mean a person wrote it?

No. When the agent runs git merge or git revert --no-edit with git's default message, or passes -m without the trailer line, the commit it makes has no trailer.

What extra commits does git log --all count?

Besides every branch and tag, it follows refs/stash, so the newest stash and its index commit count as two commits. git log --exclude=refs/stash --all leaves them out.

Can a merge commit carry a Co-Authored-By trailer?

It can if you pass the message yourself with git merge --no-ff -m "message" and put the trailer on its last line. After a merge conflict, add the same line to the git commit -m that concludes the merge.

Checked 2026-10-25. Git history of four repositories (cutoff fixed at the end of October 24, KST), Claude Code session logs kept on this PC, and the GitHub pull request list. Author names and session IDs are left out.

item.title: AI coding agents and secrets: chat, logs, tokens – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Keeping secrets away from an AI coding agent: one rule for chat, logs and token permissions

Give the agent commands that check without printing values, keep log masking in one function guarded by a test that fails on copies, and give deploy tokens only the permissions the code needs.

Giving an agent rules and limits 5/5

An AI coding agent reads files, writes code and designs deployments, and each of those opens a path for a secret to leak. Whatever it reads lands in the session log, the logging code it writes can print tokens, and the deployments it plans can ask for broader tokens than the code needs. All three paths opened for real in three SugarMount app repositories; this note shows how each was closed. The rule behind all three fits in a sentence: never copy a secret's value anywhere, only say where it is and what kind it is.

Chat: the first secrets rule was written 47 seconds after a key reached the session log

On the morning of October 2, 2026, the operator asked the agent to fill in the shared instructions every session reads. To learn the setup, it printed the last 150 lines of the shell history, and one of them exported an AI API key. Tool output is saved verbatim in the session log, so the key was now part of the transcript.

Forty-seven seconds later the agent wrote the first secrets rule into the instructions: one line saying secrets stay out of any output. It said what not to do and nothing about how to check, and for an agent, reading a file and printing it are the same action. The agent then told the operator that an AI API key sat in plain text in the shell history, giving the location and kind but not the value.

Eight minutes on, the operator asked for a rule that keeps passwords and personal data out of every session's chat, and the agent replaced the one line with a rule that also says how to check. Files are checked with commands that show key names and line counts (grep -c, cut -d= -f1), and commands take environment variables or file references instead of values. It covers commits, docs and memory files as well as chat, and a value someone pastes in is not quoted back; the agent recommends rotating it. The scope also widened to personal data.

The agent deleted the four history lines that held the key and counted again: zero. It listed what it left alone, the running session's log file, which could break if edited mid-session, and the terminal window where the key had been typed, and said that deleting doesn't undo the exposure; rotating the key is the only sure fix.

To see whether the rule changed habits, we recounted the session logs on October 25. What grew was the names-only check; counting lines was already a habit before the rule.

Lines matching three known key shapes (the newer AI API key format, GitHub tokens, sk- keys) came to exactly one across all 2,567 logs including subagents: that October 2 output.

# .env: line count and key names, no values
grep -c '=' .env
cut -d= -f1 .env
# shell history: how many lines mention that key name
grep -c 'API_KEY' ~/.bash_history
# commands reference values instead of containing them
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" https://api.example.com/v1/ping

Logs: four copies of a masking regex, and two exceptions that never masked

The chat app (Flutter) passes a shared token as ?token= in the signaling server URL. On September 7 the agent reviewing it before release rated this High: the discovery logs went through debugPrint, which prints in release builds too, and four connect-log lines wrote the whole URL.

The reviewing agent proposed Uri.parse(url).replace(query: null), which keeps the query: in Dart's Uri.replace, a null argument means "keep the existing component". The agent assigned to fix it caught that and switched to a one-line regex.

The copies came from how the work was split. Several fix agents each owned a set of files that day. The mobile owner's scope was "one masking line" in its two files, and the two web files went to another owner, where a separate _maskToken wrapped the same regex. The next day's docs said "regex duplicated in 4 files; extracting a shared helper is still open", while the defect list already said Fixed.

On September 13, writing the shared function meant looking at every place each file turned the URL into a string. Two HttpException sites in the mobile HTTP client had no masking at all: a failed connection or POST put the token into the exception message or its uri field. The mobile owner's first fix had covered the success log line only.

String maskSignalingUrl(String url) =>
    url.replaceAllMapped(_signalingToken, (m) => '${m[1]}***');
final RegExp _signalingToken = RegExp(
  r'([?&](?:token|secret)=)[^&#\s]*',
  caseSensitive: false,
);

The new pattern ignores case, also covers secret=, and stops at # or whitespace. We ran the old pattern ([?&]token=)[^&]* and the new one through Python's re on placeholder values to see the difference:

InputOld regexNew regex
ws://h/ws?TOKEN=XXXXunchanged?TOKEN=***
ws://h/ws?secret=XXXXunchanged?secret=***
ws://h/ws?token=XXXX#frag?token=*** (fragment eaten)?token=***#frag
http://h/api/token/listunchangedunchanged

Three kinds of tests went in with it: 7 rule tests, 1 source guard, and 1 real failure path. The failure-path test starts an HTTP server on the loopback address that answers 401 and checks that the client's exception text contains token=*** and not the value. The source guard, shortened:

test('no copy of the masking regex comes back in discovery', () {
  final offenders = <String>[];
  for (final f in Directory('lib/core/discovery').listSync()) {
    if (f is! File || !f.path.endsWith('.dart')) continue;
    if (f.path.endsWith('discovery_log.dart')) continue; // the definition
    final src = f.readAsStringSync();
    if (src.contains('token=)') || src.contains('_maskToken')) {
      offenders.add(f.path);
    }
  }
  expect(offenders, isEmpty);
});

It fails if the regex fragment token=) or the old helper's name shows up in any file other than the definition. The duplication stayed for five days after it was written down on September 8, so copies are now blocked by a test rather than left to review. Keep one masking function, and commit a test that fails when a copy appears.

Release logcat also carried what users typed

On October 17, QA on the SugarSpeller spell checker found the same class of bug in its release logcat, the Android device log. Up to version 1.6.030, release builds logged the check request URL (which contains the user's text), the start of the raw response, a session key for the external checking service and the push notification token. In the app's logging wrapper, log.e prints whether or not the build is a debug build.

Diagnostic lines moved to log.d, and keys and text are logged only as a length or a present/absent flag. A new test scans all main sources for log calls that print in release and looks only at interpolations and arguments outside string literals. Its first test feeds in the 7 old leaking lines and requires all 7 to be caught (the same yardstick as in Catch fake AI-written tests by deleting their guards). A release build of the next version went onto a Galaxy S20, and logcat showed zero such lines.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Permissions: the Worker was redesigned instead of adding permissions to the token

The family app keeps photos in Cloudflare R2 object storage, with a media Worker handling uploads and reads. The deploy notes of October 10 listed three jobs for a person: add Workers KV edit and billing read to the deploy token, create a separate token for the usage analytics API, and issue an R2 S3 key pair so Firebase functions could delete objects. The reason was a free-tier guard that read Cloudflare's analytics API every hour.

That night the operator told the agent to do the work itself instead of handing it over, and around midnight the agent committed a Worker that runs without any extra token. The first design, one new credential per feature, had been the agent's own; this time it rebuilt the same features on the R2 binding, the Durable Object and the shared key it already had. By design the token needs 2 permissions: Workers Scripts Edit and R2 Edit.

  • A Durable Object (a stateful object that runs next to the Worker) now counts the day's requests and R2 reads and writes itself. When the total passes a set share of the free allowance, uploads and reads close for the day and reopen at the next midnight, Korea time.
  • Functions delete R2 objects through a signed DELETE request to the Worker instead of S3 credentials. The signing key is derived from an HMAC key the functions and the Worker already shared; timestamps must be within 60 seconds, a nonce works once, and only paths under the requesting family's folder are deleted.
  • Worker secrets went from 3 to 1, and billing read was never added.

The cost is written down in the ops notes. Because the delete-signing key comes from the shared HMAC key, all 4 function service accounts that can read that key could in theory sign a delete. Narrowing it again means a separate delete key, which is one more Worker secret.

A read-only ops check the next day found the real token had 3 permissions, one more than the design: Account Settings Read. With no billing read, the plan API answered with an auth error, which also confirms this token cannot change the plan or billing.

A copy written another way passes the source guard, and masking does not protect the token

The source guard looks for two strings in one folder. A regex written another way, or a copy in another folder, passes. The spell checker's log scan works line by line, so a log call split across lines gets through.

Masking does not protect the secret itself. The chat app's token is a constant in the app binary and can be extracted, which is why the app treats it only as spam control. The review found the web client cannot send the token in a header, so the fix closed the path from URL to log instead. The chat rule works only while the agent follows it, and the count only finds key shapes we know.

The same night the Worker was reworked to need no extra token, the agent's own tool permissions grew. Its permission checker blocked the IAM grant commands, and approval in chat did not lift the block; an allow rule in the settings was required. The agent asked for lines allowing all gcloud, npx firebase-tools and curl commands, and the operator added them. How we scope what an agent may do on its own is in A permission table for a scheduled AI agent: what it does alone, and which clicks a person makes.

Checks to add to agent instructions, masking code and token scopes

  1. Put checking commands next to the prohibition in your agent instructions: grep -c, cut -d= -f1, and $NAME references in commands (on the file itself: How to write AGENTS.md: only the rules an AI coding agent gets wrong).
  2. Don't let the agent read the shell history or .env whole. Have it count the lines that mention a key name; delete any key it finds there and rotate it. Pass new values through a prompt or a file, not a command argument.
  3. For each kind of string that carries a secret (a URL, say), keep one masking function and call it everywhere that string is built: logs, exception messages, exception uri fields, diagnostics maps.
  4. Write three tests: the rules (case, other key names, fragments, the same word in a path), a source guard (regex fragments outside the definition file), and a real failure path (a 4xx from a local server).
  5. Feed a log checker the old leaking lines first and confirm it catches them.
  6. Install a release build on a real device and search logcat by key name or marker. Grepping for the value puts the value back into your shell history.
  7. For tokens, write down the permissions each feature needs, and before adding a credential check whether an existing binding or key can do the job. Confirm the real scope with read-only calls.
  8. Where something got wider, write one line: what widened, and what it would take to narrow it.
# release logcat: count token= lines that are not masked
adb logcat -d | grep 'token=' | grep -vc 'token=\*\*\*'

What is left: one stale doc line, one transcript line, one undeployed Worker

The chat app's security doc still says "regex duplicated in 4 files"; the code changed and that line did not. A key that has landed in a session log stays exposed even after the line is deleted, so rotating such a key is the default. For the family app, once the Worker is deployed, we need to confirm uploads and deletes work with the 2 designed permissions and whether the extra Account Settings Read is needed at all.

Questions, consulting or collaboration

Email us with a question about this note, consulting on app development or on adopting AI agents such as Claude Code, or a collaboration idea.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com · Subscribe via RSS

Giving an agent rules and limits: all 5 parts

  1. A permission table for a scheduled AI agent: what it does alone, and which clicks a person makes

This is the last part.

FAQ

Is it safe to let an AI coding agent read my .env file?

Not in a way that prints values. Agent tool output is stored in the session log as is. With cut -d= -f1 .env for key names and grep -c for counts, the agent can still tell whether a setting is missing.

Why is a masking regex copied into several files a problem?

What one copy handles doesn't carry over to the others. In this chat app the web copies masked failure messages too, while two failure exceptions in the mobile file sent the token unmasked. One function plus a source-guard test that fails on copies prevents it.

How do I cut down the cloud token permissions an agent uses?

List the permissions each feature needs, and before creating a credential, check whether an existing binding or shared key can do the same job.

Sources: git history and tests from three repositories (the chat app, a Korean spell checker app and a family app in development) and agent session logs, September 7 to October 25, 2026. Every secret shown is a placeholder such as XXXX.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.
