item.title: We checked the market after 3 apps: median 1,166 – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Retrospective

We built three photo apps before checking the market: this year's new apps had a median of 1,166 installs

Before building an app, check how this year's new apps in the same category are doing. We ran a four-minute scrape only after shipping three photo apps: the 32 compress apps released in 2026 had a median of 1,166 installs.

Three photo apps, the first 20 days 4/4

On the morning of October 3, 2026, three of our Android photo apps were already built and uploaded to Play. Compress Image was waiting on the production track; a flip-and-rotate app and an image format converter sat on the internal test track. The operator asked a blunt question that morning: there must be hundreds of AI-built photo apps by now, so had anyone looked at the market? Nobody had. We had the coding agent scrape Play search results, and the first report came back four minutes later. Of 71 compress-and-resize utilities in the top 30 results, 32 had been released in 2026, and their median lifetime installs were 1,166. Our own app was not in the top 30 for any of the nine queries.

Sources: three market research documents in the app repository (2026-10-03), the ops check of 2026-10-23, git history and the work log. Install counts are the worldwide lifetime numbers Play shows. Checked on October 24, 2026.

26 of the 32 compress apps released this year had fewer than 10,000 installs

The compress category came first. Six Korean and three English queries, top 30 results each, gave 103 apps. Keeping only utilities whose titles mention compressing, file size or resizing left 71. Of those, 47 were released in 2025 or 2026, and 32 in 2026.

Those 32 topped out at 73,286 installs. None had reached 100,000, and 26 were under 10,000. One 2026 app that aimed at exactly our pitch, getting photos ready for upload forms, had 0. The top of the list belonged to apps released between 2013 and 2022; the leader had 43.06 million installs.

About ninety minutes later the agent ran the same scrape for the other two categories. Flip and rotate: 46 utilities, only 7 released in 2026, median 373. Format conversion: 71 utilities, 38 from 2026, median 136. In none of the three categories had a 2026 app passed 100,000.

Twenty days later, in the October 23 ops check, the download badges on the public Play pages read 5+ for Compress Image, 1+ for the flip app and 0+ for the converter. Those are 20-day-old apps, so they cannot be lined up against lifetime counts that had up to ten months to build. We read them only as a slow start.

We skipped the check because building looked cheaper than checking

The missing check had a chain of causes behind it.

The lineup was chosen by feature. The product spec revised on September 21 fixed a list of 14 apps and paired each candidate with a "reference app" from one established developer. The same section said, in its own words, that the order was not a download ranking or a revenue forecast.

The reference apps then created an illusion. The reference compress app had 3.89 million installs, and the top of the search results was apps from 2013 to 2022 with millions to tens of millions of installs. If you only look at survivors, "build the same thing, but cleaner" sounds like a plan. Nobody looked at what happened to the apps that arrived this year.

The biggest link was cost: building had become very cheap. The flip-and-rotate app went from its engine commit (September 24, 13:29) to the internal test track (20:51) in 7 hours 22 minutes, and the converter reached the internal track at 22:39 the same night. Leaving out review and store listing work, an app took less than a day, so "ship it and read the numbers" sounded reasonable. The scrape took four minutes.

Underneath all three: the workflow had no gate that said "look at the market before you build". It had a release gate and on-device checks, both described in Claude Code for Android app development: 4 apps in 20 days, but nothing upstream of the code.

None of our three starting assumptions was supported by the data

Assumption one: an app that fixes what users hate about the incumbents will get installs. In the newest reviews of the top six compress apps, 127 were rated 3 stars or lower. Keyword tagging put 39 of them under too many ads, 19 under errors, 17 under paid plans and subscriptions, and 12 under output that missed the target size. Our app has no subscription and never writes a file larger than the original. Yet 26 of this year's 32 entrants had not reached 10,000 installs. That figure does not split apps that fixed the complaints from apps that did not, so it cannot refute the assumption directly. It does not support it either. (The top complaint applied to us too: the agent reported that the app-open ad turned on in 1.0.3 on September 23, an operator decision, was the same type. The operator kept it.)

Assumption two came from the operator: merge the three apps into one photo toolbox and people will look for it. The agent searched Play for Korean phrases meaning "photo tool set", "photo utilities" and "image tools", plus "image toolbox" in English. The top results were the default photo app, gallery apps and big photo editors. What the data shows is that general apps own the category-name searches. Play hides search volume, so we do not know how many people search that way.

That afternoon the same question went to document viewers. One developer had three apps: a viewer for HWP files (the Korean word processor format that government offices use) at 436k installs, a PowerPoint viewer at 469k, and an all-in-one office app at 13k. Three apps from one developer, with HWP demand boosted by a policy change, cannot prove that single-purpose beats all-in-one; we treated it as a directional signal. Assumption three, that AI features would make a viewer stand out, was checked against reviews. Of 15,043 Korean reviews of document viewers, 0.36% asked for AI, summaries or translation. That says reviewers rarely ask for it, not that AI cannot set an app apart. Both signals pointed the same way, so the next app became a single-purpose HWP viewer, HWP Viewer SugarDoc.

The agent followed the spec's order, and got the median wrong

The coding agent executed the spec's order as written. While shipping the third app it never suggested looking at the market before the next one. When the operator asked, the agent admitted no market analysis had been done and pointed at the spec's "not a forecast" line.

The numbers had a small error too. Re-reading the scrape script for this note, we found the median computed as s[len(s)//2] on the sorted list s. With 32 values that returns the upper of the two middle values, 1,304. The true median, the mean of 1,028 and 1,304, is 1,166, and that is the number this note uses. The conclusion stands. The flip category has 7 values, so its 373 is exact. The converter category has 38, so its 136 is also an upper median; the value list was not kept, so we could not recompute it, and the true figure is 136 or lower.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

We recorded 11 planned apps as on hold and changed category

There were four options on the table.

  • Keep building the other 11 planned apps. If those categories look like the three photo ones, that repeats the same result eleven times. We have not scraped any of them yet, though. The hold was recorded in the backlog on October 4.
  • Buy installs with ads. Not until we have measured what one install is worth.
  • Unpublish the three apps. Keeping them up costs almost nothing, and the search terms people actually used only show up in Play Console after an app is public. They stay up for a 30-day measurement.
  • Move to a category where demand is shifting. From October 2026, Korean government mail systems block .hwp attachments, which pushes documents to the newer HWPX format. One viewer released in May 2026 had already reached 417,538 installs. This is the one we chose.

There were other ways to check the market, too. Paid app-intelligence services show install trends and estimated keyword data, for a subscription fee. Keyword tools can only estimate Play search volume, because Play does not publish it. Skimming the top-chart pages by hand is free, but the chart tops do not show how this year's entrants are doing. The record does not say why a script was chosen. What it does show is that the agent was already working in the repository and the cost was a few minutes.

The HWP viewer was started on October 4, went public on October 10, and shipped with no ad SDK. The difference from the photo apps is that review data and a rendering spike came before the first line of app code. (The rendering spike is written up in Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents.)

Before you build your next app, look at the median installs of this year's entrants in the same category.

The 15-minute check to run before building

This is the order we ran on October 3, plus step 2 (writing the rule first), which we skipped that day. Collection used the Python library google-play-scraper, which reads Play's web pages; it is not an official Google API.

  1. Write 6 to 9 queries in task words, the way a user would type them. We used six Korean queries and three English ones, such as "compress image" and "image resize kb".
  2. Write the decision rule before looking. For example: if this year's entrants have a median in the low thousands and none has passed 100,000, do not build a single-feature general utility.
  3. Collect the top 30 app IDs per query. For each app read lifetime installs, release date, rating count, and whether it has ads or in-app purchases.
  4. Keep only apps whose title names the same task. We excluded general photo editors, video apps and PDF apps with a deny list. 103 became 71.
  5. Take the apps released this year and count them, plus their median installs (mean of the two middle values when the count is even), maximum, how many are under 10,000 and how many are over 100,000. Note the release years of the top 10.
  6. Check whether your own app ID appears anywhere in the results.
  7. Pull up to 200 of the newest reviews for each of the top six apps, keep 3 stars and lower, and tag them by keyword: ads, payment, errors.
  8. Search once more with the category name ("photo utilities"). If you are considering an all-in-one app, look at that result first.

Below is a cleaned-up version of the collection code from that day, arranged to follow steps 3 to 6. We have not run this cleaned-up version, only syntax-checked it, so adapt the queries and both regexes to your category. The median comes from statistics.median, the line that prevents the upper-median mistake described above.

import re, statistics, time
from google_play_scraper import search, app
QUERIES = [("사진 용량 줄이기", "ko", "kr"), ("사진 KB 줄이기", "ko", "kr"), ("compress image", "en", "us")]
KEEP = re.compile(r"압축|용량|크기|사이즈|compress|resiz|kb|size", re.I)
DROP = re.compile(r"video|동영상|pdf|editor|편집", re.I)
YEAR, MY_APP = 2026, "com.example.myapp"
ids = set()
for q, lang, country in QUERIES:
    ids |= {r["appId"] for r in search(q, lang=lang, country=country, n_hits=30) if r.get("appId")}
    time.sleep(1)
rows = []
for app_id in sorted(ids):
    try:
        d = app(app_id, lang="ko", country="kr")
    except Exception:
        continue
    time.sleep(0.4)
    name = f'{d.get("title") or ""} {app_id}'
    if not KEEP.search(name) or DROP.search(name):
        continue
    m = re.search(r"\d{4}", d.get("released") or "")   # "Oct 3, 2026" or "2026. 10. 3."
    rows.append((int(m.group()) if m else None, d.get("realInstalls") or 0))
new = [n for y, n in rows if y == YEAR]
print("same-task apps:", len(rows), "| released in", YEAR, ":", len(new))
if new:
    print("median", statistics.median(new), "| max", max(new),
          "| under 10k", sum(n < 10_000 for n in new), "| 100k+", sum(n >= 100_000 for n in new))
print("my app in results:", MY_APP in ids)

The four minutes cover collection and the first report for one category (09:47 to 09:51 Korea time). Add choosing queries and a person reading the tables against the step 2 rule, and budget 15 minutes.

Why the median is not a forecast, and what the data cannot see

The sample itself leans one way. Only apps in the top 30 for the nine queries got in; this year's apps that never ranked were left out. The median for all same-task apps released this year is probably below 1,166. So 1,166 is the result for this year's apps that made the top of search, and cannot be read as what a well-made app should expect. Even among them, six passed 10,000, the largest at 73,286.

In a category where demand is moving, last year's distribution says little about next month. Document viewers were that case: right after the policy change, new apps were collecting hundreds of thousands of installs.

Installs are worldwide lifetime counts, and rankings come from a logged-out session, so a real user's screen may differ. Review topics were counted with keyword regexes, so one review can land in several topics, and only six apps' newest reviews were read. Apps with an empty release-date field drop out of the yearly count. The library depends on Play's page layout and breaks when that changes.

What we check next

The 30-day measurement for Compress Image (through November 2, 2026) is not in this note yet. Impressions, install conversion and the real search terms will decide whether the three photo apps get merged into one. As of October 24, 2026 that merge has not started.

None of the 11 held categories (photo to PDF, video, audio and others) has been scraped yet. Whether the hold is right can only be judged after running the same check on them, and the operator has not formally confirmed the hold. The next scrape runs with the median fixed.

Questions, consulting or collaboration

Email us with a question about this note, consulting on app development or on adopting AI agents such as Claude Code, or a collaboration idea.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com · Subscribe via RSS

Three photo apps, the first 20 days: all 4 parts

  1. Fitting a JPEG under a file size limit: quality binary search, a predicted long edge, and a final check against the original

This is the last part.

Frequently asked questions

How many installs does a new Android utility app usually get?

In the photo-compress category we scraped on October 3, 2026, the 32 apps released that year that made the top 30 search results had a median of 1,166 lifetime installs. It varies by category, so scrape your own before building.

Can I see Google Play search volume for a keyword?

No. Play does not publish search volume per query. After your app is public, Play Console shows only the search terms that brought users to your own listing.

Does an all-in-one app beat single-feature apps on Play?

Our data showed no sign that it does. A category search like "photo utilities" returned only general apps, and one developer's two single-format viewers had 436k and 469k installs against 13k for its all-in-one app. That is one developer, so we do not treat it as a rule.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • Claude Code on WSL vs native Windows: what changed after the move
  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException

item.title: One --check gate for a static site agents co-edit – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Keeping a static site safe when several AI agents edit it: one --check before every commit

Commit only when a fresh rebuild would change zero files and the checks report zero errors. That one rule catches the problems that appear only after separate pieces of work are combined.

Many agents, one repository 4/6

When several AI coding agent sessions work in one repository, each can verify its own change and the combined result can still break. This site has no framework: a build script written against the Python standard library generates it, and whoever commits, person or agent, first passes python tools/build.py --check. Between October 5 and 22, 2026, that command stopped a commit four times. Here is what it caught and the rules that came out of it.

Four times --check stopped a commit

--check rebuilds the whole site in memory and asks two questions. Does any output differ by even one byte from the file on disk? Did the checker module, tools/checks.py, report an error? Either one means exit 1, and nothing is written.

outputs = build_all()              # pages, feeds, sitemap, CSS: in memory
changed = [p for p, text in outputs.items()
           if read_file(p) != text]
report = checks.run(ROOT, outputs)  # 106 issue codes
if "--check" in argv:
    if changed or report.errors:
        exit(1)                     # nothing is written
else:
    write_files(changed)

On October 24 a run produced 162 files, ran 106 named checks and took 11.6 seconds. The four stops:

DateWhat failedCause
Oct 5Two files out of date right after the first buildDates read from git state
Oct 18101 gate errors at the redesign integrationMostly the checker miscounting
Oct 19Home page needed 421 KB of fonts, cap 400 KBDaily-changing note titles, merged in by a rebase
Oct 22Two older notes at 482 KB and 473 KB, cap 470 KBOne rare syllable in a new note's title

None of the four shows up when you check a single file. They were caught because the whole output was rebuilt and compared.

Humans and agents write only the body and the data files

Every file has exactly one kind of writer. Condensed from the table in the repository's AGENTS.md, the instruction file agents read before they start:

WriterFiles
Content authors (people or agents)The <title>, description and <main> of hand-written pages (minus build blocks), data JSON
One build-owner sessionThe build code, and the one integration build
The build onlyHead, header, footer, breadcrumbs, JSON-LD, list pages, sitemap, RSS, the dates file, generated CSS

Inside a hand-written page, every spot the build fills is wrapped in a marker such as <!-- build:meta -->. Each build empties and refills only those blocks and leaves the rest of <main> byte for byte. Content authors never run the build; they run the read-only single-file check, tools/checks.py --file.

The first plan did not have this split. An agent wrote the October 18 redesign spec, and it told every work package both to finish with build and --check and to leave generated HTML alone. A second agent, assigned to attack the spec, pointed out the contradiction: the build rewrites the head and footer of every hand-written page, so one session building to verify its work would change some 60 files another session was editing. Since then the integration build runs once, in one place.

Rebase conflicts follow the same rule. On October 19 the conflicted files were all ones the build rewrites: 404.html, the about page, app pages, rss.xml. Do not hand-merge generated files. Pick a side, rebuild, and commit only when --check reports zero.

Test idempotency with tomorrow's date, not with a second build

On October 5 an agent wrote the first build script and ran it. This came back:

45 files, 45 changed
out of date:
  apps/sugarcard/index.html
  sitemap.xml

A second build changed two files, and the third said up to date. The lines that moved were sitemap lastmod dates.

There were two layers of cause. The near one was ordering: the build read dates from git status and git log before writing anything, so its own writes changed the input of the next run. The deeper one was the source of the date itself, which was repository state and the wall clock instead of page content.

That day's fix addressed only the near cause. Two builds on the same day then agreed, but the same input built the next day still moved the dates. A build that converges after two runs is not idempotent.

Thirteen days later the redesign switched to dates derived from a hash of the page body. The redesign spec, also written by an agent, had two loops of the same kind: a date line inside the hashed body, so date and hash kept changing each other, and a CSS version string that hashed the very file the build writes into. The reviewer wrote that --check would "fail once, forever". Both were fixed before any code was written. The date rules are in Every sitemap lastmod had the same date: deriving modified dates from a content hash.

The build's idea of "today" can now be overridden with a SOURCE_DATE environment variable. A run in a scratch copy on October 24:

$ SOURCE_DATE=2026-10-25 python tools/build.py
162 files, 0 changed
$ SOURCE_DATE=2026-12-31 python tools/build.py
162 files, 0 changed

At the first integration, the gate was the one that was wrong

The October 18 redesign was split across 36 agents and took 2 hours 24 minutes. The first --check on the merged result found zero files to rewrite and 101 gate errors.

Most of the 43 font-budget errors were the checker's own mistake. English pages draw © in the system font through CSS, but the checker counted that character and decided the pages needed extra font files. One cost was real: the breadcrumb separator › alone made every page download one more 25 KB font file. The fix aligned the checker's counting with the CSS rules and moved the separator to the system font.

When the gate changes, its tests change with it. That fix added six tests, and each of the eight new guards was removed in turn in a scratch copy to confirm a test failed. As of October 24, every one of the 106 checks is named in a test.

The integrating agent also loosened the gate twice on its own. Two kinds of pages with no cap in the spec got font overruns as warnings only, and the cap on the generated font stylesheet went from 20 KB to 24 KB. It marked both "needs confirmation" in its report; by October 24 nobody had confirmed either.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Another note's title can break a page's font budget

The site's Korean font is split into 92 files, and a page downloads only the files that cover its characters. Note pages are capped at 470 KB, home and list pages at 400 KB. One rare Hangul syllable can pull in a 17 to 40 KB file by itself, so two of the first three AX notes went over and were reworded that evening.

The home page broke for another reason. It listed the three newest note titles, which changed every day, and after the rebase merged another session's work it needed 421 KB. Instead of rewording titles, the home list became links to topic pages, whose names never change. Dropping note titles from the topic cards on the AX notes front page on October 22 had the same reason and took that page from 468 KB to 389 KB.

Also on October 22, a single syllable, 쟀, in a new note's title travelled through the related-notes lists into two older notes and pushed them to 482 KB and 473 KB. Checking the new file alone passes. Rewording the title brought the two pages to 450 KB and 441 KB.

Images are still outside the gate

tools/og.py builds share images from real Play screenshots on a neutral background, and --check does not rebuild or compare them. Running og.py in a scratch copy on October 24 changed 4 of 155 files. Two runs in a row give identical bytes, so the files that differ are the ones committed without going through the generator. The story behind the blank-glyph check in the image tools is in Android showed some Hangul as blank gaps: NanumSquare's cmap claimed 11,172 syllables but drew only 2,479.

Not for browser editing, very large sites or repositories without CI

Teams that write in a browser and expect a preview will not like it; here authors edit the HTML body directly and run commands. A static site generator would not remove the need for this gate: three of the four stops came from checks over the whole output, so you would still build those checks and the date rules yourself.

Large sites pay more. --check rebuilds and compares everything on every run, with no incremental build.

Nothing enforces the gate. The repository has no CI, so it works only if someone runs the command before committing. The gate can also be wrong, and it cannot stop a commit that raises its own caps.

Adding a --check gate to another site, in order

  1. Put a table of who writes which files at the top of your agent instructions, and mark generated files as hands-off.
  2. Wrap every spot the build fills inside a hand-written page in <!-- build:NAME --> markers; the build empties and refills them each time.
  3. Make --check render every output in memory, compare it with disk, run the checks on the same output, and exit 1 if either fails.
  4. Derive dates and version strings from content hashes, and keep date lines and automatic lists out of the hash input.
  5. Test idempotency with two builds in a row, a build dated tomorrow and one dated in the past.
  6. Give every check a fixed code and a test that proves it fires; remove each guard in a scratch copy and confirm a test fails.
  7. Content sessions run only the per-file check; one session runs the integration build once. When generated files conflict in a rebase, pick a side and rebuild.
  8. Check budgets that mix in other pages' text (fonts, size) on the whole output, and keep daily-changing lists off shared pages.
  9. Have a person review any commit that changes a cap.

What we will check next

The next step is a stage in --check that compares og.py output with the committed images. Before that, the app cards that carry text have to become either a listed exception or generator output. The 24 KB stylesheet cap and the two warning-only page types still need a human review.

Questions, consulting or collaboration

Email us with a question about this note, consulting on app development or on adopting AI agents such as Claude Code, or a collaboration idea.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com · Subscribe via RSS

Many agents, one repository: all 6 parts

  1. Multiple Claude Code sessions in one repo: a file owner table
  2. Every branch passed its AI review, and the merged code still had 12 defects

Frequently asked questions

Do you commit the generated HTML?

Yes. GitHub Pages serves the repository's files as they are, so the build output is the deployment. --check confirms that the committed output equals what the current inputs produce.

How do you test that a static site build is idempotent?

Build twice in a row, then with tomorrow's date and with a past date, and expect zero changed files. For that, the build's "today" has to be overridable through an environment variable.

How do you resolve conflicts when several AI agent sessions edit the same site repository?

Merge only source files such as page bodies and data; for generated files, pick one side and rebuild. Commit only when --check passes on the rebuilt result. On this site, that step is where the home page font overflow first appeared.

Sources: this site's git history and build code, the review documents written against the redesign spec, and work session logs (October 5 to 24, 2026). Home page captured November 13, 2026.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • Verifying an AI agent's "done" report: 95.2% vs a 92.3% cap

item.title: HWP save gate caught a bug, so edit shipped off – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

We built an edit feature and shipped it switched off: the HWP save gate that caught a form-field bug

The pre-save gate blocked both form-field saves, so we shipped 1.1.0 with editing switched off by a build flag and turned it on nine days later in 1.3.0, without form fields.

Building the SugarDoc HWP viewer 6/8

If you build a feature that edits and saves documents and your pre-save check keeps rejecting the output, cutting the feature's scope is safer than loosening the check. Every time someone filled a form field in an HWP document and saved it in HWP Viewer SugarDoc, the pre-save gate refused the save. On October 9, 2026, an end-to-end run on a Galaxy S20 showed it on both form-field test documents. The record diff showed the engine rewriting paragraphs the user never edited. That day we shipped 1.1.0 to the internal track with editing turned off by a build flag, and nine days later 1.3.0 turned it on without form fields.

Filling a field made rhwp rewrite paragraphs nobody edited

HWP is the file format of the Hangul word processor. SugarDoc edits it by running the open-source rhwp 0.8.6 engine in a WebView, and it only ever writes the result to a new file; the received original is never written. Before saving, a Kotlin verifier compares the exported bytes with the original, record by record. The set of changed paragraphs must equal the set of paragraphs the user edited.

Replaying the same edit on a PC and diffing the records showed three changes. In the filled field's control header record (CTRL_HEADER, tag 71), an attribute byte went from 0x01 to 0x80. One tag-69 record in that paragraph disappeared. Third, field-end character ids were rewritten in other paragraphs the user never touched (clk+0x0109 became %clk+0). The gate saw that and blocked the save with PARAGRAPHS control record tag 71 changed. (The device runs typed with adb input text, so the markers were ASCII strings like ZQ…; Korean input was not checked.)

On screen the filled text looked fine. Without the gate, filling one blank would have produced a file whose other paragraphs had different field data.

The first plan trusted the engine's verify function, which only counts pages

The product spec's line for editing said: save only if exportHwpVerify passes. The edit spike broke that assumption. The function compares page counts and nothing else. It returned "recovered":true when an old HWP3 document lost content and when a distribution-protected document silently lost its protection. Its loss report (contentLoss) said zero in every case.

So we wrote our own verifier. The core of the paragraph verdict, condensed from the repository code:

// HwpExportVerifier, per section (condensed from the repo)
paragraph key = (section, paragraph index[, table control / cell / cell paragraph path])
original and result paragraph counts differ        → GATE_PARAGRAPHS
for each pair a (original), b (result) at the same position:
    key or nesting level differs                    → fail
    control record differs outside the allow-list   → "control record tag N changed"
    all paragraph records identical                 → next
    a.key in edited paragraphs (ops)                → add to changed, run edited-paragraph checks
    within the edited section's re-serialization allow-list → next
    otherwise                                       → "unedited paragraph changed"
edited paragraphs - changed is not empty            → fail
// EditWiringTest (1.1.0): release builds ship with edit off
if (!BuildConfig.DEBUG) assertEquals(false, BuildConfig.FLAG_EDIT)

The allow-list came from round trips with no edits at all. One document differed in 43 LIST_HEADER (tag 72) records even when nothing was edited.

One of our own assumptions was wrong too. The first size check rejected results under half the original size. Fifteen unedited saves came out at 0.05 to 0.48 times the original with identical records and images; the engine had simply dropped empty sectors in Hancom-written files. We removed the lower bound. The check is cheap: saving one edit to a 77-page document took 3.6 s on the S20 (4.9 s in a fresh process) and 5.1 s on the S21, against a 10 s limit.

None of the 2,899 corpus edits filled a form field

Before the device run, the PC corpus looked good. In a corpus of 164 HWP5 documents, twenty random edits on each editable document passed 2,662 of 2,899 times, and no passing result hid a difference outside the allow-list. The corpus generator was a script the agent wrote alongside the edit feature, and it produced only two kinds of edit: body text runs and table cell text. The E2E report put it plainly: the edit corpus (random run edits) had no field fills, so it missed this.

The agent that ran the edit spike had recommended "filling body form fields" as part of the scope, because the setFieldValue API existed and filled values survived a save on a PC. The device run reversed that recommendation, 2 failures out of 2.

The same hole showed up again. In the E2E before 1.3.0, typing into an empty paragraph with no controls always failed with GATE_CONTROLS, at all 7 empty paragraphs of one document. Empty paragraphs have no text runs, so random run edits could never pick them. Both times the generator picked edit positions from the text runs the engine rendered, not from the list of edit kinds the UI offers.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

We shrank the feature instead of widening the gate

Do not ship a feature the gate blocks by loosening the gate. Cut the scope, or ship it behind a flag that is off. For the form-field defect we had three options:

  • Allow the three changes. The third one alters unedited paragraphs, so it breaks the rule that changed paragraphs equal edited paragraphs. Doing it safely means normalizing field-end ids on the comparison side and adding field fills to the corpus first. Moved to a later release.
  • Patch the engine. rhwp is pinned to 0.8.6 by hash, and the design note says to normalize in the comparison, not in rhwp.
  • Block the field. Tapping a field shows "This form field can't be filled in yet." instead of the edit sheet, and the event doc_edit_blocked reason=field counts demand. We took this one.

Blocking fields did not make edit ready. Three decisions were still open: whether free users see the menu item, the price of Pro with editing, and whether Hancom Office, the suite that makes HWP, opens our files. Finding an edit target with TalkBack was not built yet either. Holding the small items (source-app chip, hiding other apps' overlays, a low-storage banner) until edit was ready was rejected too: the design document estimated about 3 days for those small items against about 19 days for edit.

That left flagEdit=false in the build config. With it off, the overflow menu has no Edit item, there is no edit mode, and the Pro panel drops its edit line. A test pins the release value to false, and all 12 new guard rows failed on a tree copy with the guard deleted (the method is in Catch fake AI-written tests by deleting their guards). 1.1.0 passed 446 release unit tests and went to the internal track on October 9. Minified release builds on the S20 and S21 had no Edit item.

On October 18 the operator picked the three open answers: free users see Edit with a Pro badge, the price stays, and the agent checks Hancom compatibility on the S21. That evening one commit (39 files) set flagEdit=true. All 1,254 unit tests passed with no failures, and the same commit added one automatic retry when the gate fails: reopen the original, replay the edits, check again.

A person was needed in two places. Re-saving in Hancom Docs needs an account login, and the agent's rules forbid entering passwords, so the two files were checked only after the operator signed in on the S21 and turned on file access. TalkBack double-tap could not be automated because adb taps bypass TalkBack, so the operator tried it by hand.

When this approach does not fit

Without a parser that reads the output independently of the engine, there is nothing to compare records with. SugarDoc already had an HWP container parser from the viewer; the record verifier was new.

If the engine changes files even when nothing is edited, the gate blocks the whole feature, not one defect. For HWPX, 0 of 34 unedited round trips passed (rhwp dropped image references and some attributes), so HWPX editing was cut entirely. In the corpus, 8.2% of HWP5 edits were blocked, concentrated in 12 documents where the engine dropped paragraphs or reordered controls; how many of those were not real damage was never sorted out. The single retry added in 1.3.0 targets something else: failures left by undo and snapshot state, recovered by reopening the original. How often it helps has not been counted yet.

Matching structure does not prove another app will open the file. Before release we only saw the 7 output files open in Hancom Office Viewer, which cannot save; the Hancom Docs re-save was checked after the production release, for 2 files. A release build cannot turn on Pro, so "flag off plus a Pro user" was never seen on a device and is covered by tests only. The disabled edit code and strings still ship in the APK.

A save-gate checklist for features that write files

  1. Test the engine's own verify function first. Feed it inputs that lose data (old formats, protected files) and see whether it reports failure.
  2. Measure no-edit round trips across the whole corpus before anything else, and allow only the differences found there. Check "obvious" limits such as size ratios at this step.
  3. Make the rule "set of changed units = set of user edits", not "no more than the number of edits".
  4. Generate the corpus from the list of edit kinds the UI offers, and add a test that each kind appears at least once.
  5. Run device E2E for each edit kind on real form documents, and set and measure a save-time limit on the largest document.
  6. When the gate blocks, reproduce it on a PC with a record diff, then block that edit's entry point instead of widening the gate.
  7. Ship anything still blocked behind a build flag, pin the release value and "no menu, no entry point" with tests, and delete the guard once to watch those tests fail.
  8. When turning it on, change the flag line and the pinned test in the same commit.

What to check next

We have not yet counted how often reason=field fired. Whether to reopen form-field filling waits on that number. If it reopens, field-end normalization goes into the comparison and field fills plus empty-paragraph edits go into the corpus first. Re-saving the other 5 output files in Hancom, and the desktop Hangul word processor, are still open. Engine measurements for the same app are in Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents.

Questions, consulting or collaboration

Email us with a question about this note, consulting on app development or on adopting AI agents such as Claude Code, or a collaboration idea.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com · Subscribe via RSS

Building the SugarDoc HWP viewer: all 8 parts

  1. We pressed BACK at seven moments before shipping one 'Save as PDF' button
  2. Seven edited HWP files in Hancom's Android apps: 7 of 7 opened, and the re-save waited for a human sign-in

FAQ

Can editing an HWP file in an Android app corrupt it?

SugarDoc compares the result with the original record by record before saving and refuses to save if anything changed outside the edited paragraphs. It never writes the received original; edits always go to a new file. Re-saving edited files in Hancom Docs was checked with two files on October 18, 2026.

Can SugarDoc fill in HWP form fields?

Not as of October 23, 2026. Version 1.3.0 edits body text and table cell text in HWP 5 documents; tapping a form field shows a notice that it cannot be filled yet. HWPX documents cannot be edited yet either.

How do you prove a feature flag really hides a feature in the release build?

Pin the release value with a test, add tests that the menu item and entry points are absent, then delete the guard and confirm those tests fail. SugarDoc also installed minified release builds on an S20 and an S21 and checked by eye that the Edit item was missing.

Sources: the SugarDoc repository's device E2E report (2026-10-09), the 1.1.0 and 1.3.0 release records, the save-gate section of the design document and the git history (as of October 23).

item.title: A permission table for a scheduled AI agent – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · How-to

A permission table for a scheduled AI agent: what it does alone, and which clicks a person makes

We split the agent's work into three lanes in one file: what it does alone, what it does after approval, and the clicks a person makes even after approving. Every scheduled run reads that file first.

Giving an agent rules and limits 4/5

An AI coding agent such as Claude Code can rerun the same prompt at set times. Those runs happen while nobody is watching, so rules given in chat never reach them; only a file the run reads does. Since October 17, 2026, SugarMount has had the agent market Arrow Knots and Block Turn this way, four times a day, with the final click on money, accounts and policy left to a person. Even an ad restart the operator had approved was blocked by the tool's permission check, and a person switched it on.

The table started with three columns and a list of stop conditions

The schedule is one morning market check and three work blocks a day. The first sentence of the work-block prompt says to read the operating rules file first; the rest says to pick the most urgent item from the to-do list, work on it within the permissions, and update the posting log and the day's report. The permission table is one section of that rules file.

The first column is what the agent may do alone: measurement, analysis, drafts, posting from accounts that already exist, and replying to comments on its own posts. Posting comes with numbers: at most two promotional posts a day, at least three days between posts on the same site, and always say you are the developer. The second column needs the operator's approval: anything that costs money (restarting ads, budget or bid changes, paid services), new sign-ups, logins and CAPTCHAs, policy declarations, and entering a real name or contact details. The third column is what the agent never does: fake accounts, rating manipulation, channels whose cost or eligibility is unchecked, and channels the operator has closed.

Below the table sit five stop conditions, copied as they are into the template further down. When one applies, the agent does not act. It marks the item Blocked and writes the options and a recommendation at the top of the daily report under "needs your decision". The numeric limits worked too: on October 18 the posting log shows "two promotional posts today, limit reached" after the second post, and nothing else went up that day.

Rules given in chat never reached the scheduled runs

It started on the evening of October 8. The operator told the agent to do all of it, and the agent replied that it would begin by creating an ads account and linking Google Play. Five minutes later the operator said: anything that spends money or looks odd, ask first. That one line was the first rule.

It only caught the moment of payment, and the trouble up to October 10 involved no money at all. Reddit had removed all our posts, and on the 10th a Korean community board suspended the account on its first post, as advertising. We traced it to new accounts dropping the same link in several places at once, and set the two-a-day and three-day limits. On October 13 the agent pushed ahead with the Galaxy Store without confirming cost or eligibility; only after two release builds were ready did the portal say Android apps need a paid seller account, and the channel was dropped. So the trigger changed from "payment" to categories, and those became the five stop conditions.

Where a rule lives mattered too. The October 8 rule sat only in the memory of a different working folder, so the marketing session never loaded it (what a long session reloads is in What survives Claude Code auto-compaction: the summary, recent files and the memory index). The only place a rule reliably reaches every run is a file the prompt names. It is the same idea as How to write AGENTS.md: only the rules an AI coding agent gets wrong, except that this table governs work outside the repository.

A tool permission check sits between approval and the click

Claude Code's auto mode asks a permission classifier before it runs a click or a command. In the marketing session the classifier refused 11 actions between October 17 and 20.

The most common reason covered making a Short public, uploading a promo image and saving a store listing. The refusals with no reason hit submitting listing changes for review and a publish step, and the shared-resources refusal stopped a command that would have changed a setting on every connected test phone.

On the afternoon of October 18 the operator said to finish everything, yet the custom store listing's submit and save buttons were refused, and they only passed after the operator asked for the save again. At 17:06 the operator approved the rest of the batch, and a minute later the click on the ad status menu came back with Permission for this action was denied by the Claude Code auto mode classifier. Reason: [Real-World Transactions]. Fourteen seconds later the same reason blocked an emulator boot check that had nothing to do with ads. In the end the operator switched the ad on.

So the approval column really splits in two: work the agent finishes once approved, and clicks a person makes even after approving. Between October 17 and 22 the posting log has seven lines where a permission check pushed the final step to a person. On October 22 an update post on a Korean gaming community sat fully filled in while the operator pressed only the submit button. Do not have the agent hunt for a workaround on a click that spends money, even after approval. Put it in the person's lane from the start, and have the agent say so the moment it is blocked.

Where the agent got it wrong: a report 3 hours 38 minutes late, and log times that were off

The ad click was blocked at 17:07, but the agent told the operator it needed a person at 20:45. In between it said nothing about the block and moved on to the rest of the approved batch, an emulator test, where one connection check waited more than three hours for a reply. That ran against the memory rule it had written 26 minutes earlier: when a check blocks you, do not leave the tab open and move on, ask right away. Now a refused click marks only that item Blocked, and it shows up at the top of that day's report under "needs your decision".

The log times were wrong as well. The posting log records the episode as "18:40 restart attempted, on hold" and "20:00 switched on, running"; the transcript says blocked at 17:07 and reported at 20:45. The agent wrote both lines later, from memory. On October 20 it logged an Instagram share as on hold after the share button was refused; the next day the post turned out to be live already.

It also erred in the timid direction. In the October 18 performance report the agent proposed posting to the community boards only at updates, where views sat around 100 to 200, and dropping one channel if its next video also got zero views. The operator corrected it: free channels grow by steady accumulation. Its memory now says: never propose cutting a channel; when results are weak, propose a different format.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

What we dropped, and what we did not use

Asking before every action never fit. The runs happen while nobody is watching, and even now one release approval and one ad decision sat at the top of the daily report for four days. Leaving it all to the tool's permission check failed too: the classifier knows nothing of two posts a day, three days per site or closed channels, it blocked posts the table allows, and 3 of its 11 refusals came with no reason.

Claude Code has its own permission controls: allow and deny rules in settings.json, and hooks that run a script just before a tool call. The user settings for these runs had neither (checked October 23). Those rules match tool names and command patterns. Marketing work is mostly browser clicks, so a click on a publish button looks like any other click to them, and counting two posts a day would need a hook that keeps its own state. Work that a command pattern can catch, such as a release script, is held more firmly by a deny rule than by a document.

Running the agent from an OS scheduler outside the session is the other option. There is no session end and no seven-day expiry, so no runs get lost. The cost is the hand-off: the agent leaves a filled-in browser tab and a person presses the last button, and that flow has to be built separately. This time we used session jobs and kept the expiry date in the table so they get registered again.

When this does not fit

The biggest limit is that the schedule lives inside the session. The registration output read "Session-only (not written to disk, dies when Claude exits). Auto-expires after 7 days." On October 22 the session ended during a move to a new development setup, and the morning check and the morning work block were skipped. If a job must never miss a day, use a scheduler outside the session.

It also fails if nobody reads the daily report. Pending decisions pile up and the important work stops first. The two-a-day and three-day numbers were set for a few Korean gaming boards; other channels need numbers from their own rules. Work full of logins, CAPTCHAs and locked phones stays largely manual whatever the table says.

How to set it up: a permission table template

This skeleton takes the three columns above and splits approval in two, giving four lanes. Copy it into a file and name that file in the first sentence of every scheduled prompt. Write the date of the incident behind each row; later, that date tells you whether the row can go.

# Permission table (every scheduled run reads this file first and follows it)
Schedule expires: YYYY-MM-DD / register again on: YYYY-MM-DD
## 1. Agent alone
- (task) | limit: _ a day, _ days apart per site | added: YYYY-MM-DD
## 2. Agent after approval
- (task) | added:
## 3. A person clicks, even after approving
- status changes that spend money
- final clicks a permission check refused (fill everything in, leave the tab open)
## 4. Never
- (task) | added:
## Stop and ask (if any applies, do not act)
- a kind of work done for the first time
- work on weak evidence
- anything publicly visible
- anything hard to undo
- anything touching money, accounts or policy
-> mark Blocked; options and a recommendation at the top of the report
## When blocked
- login, CAPTCHA or permission denial: Blocked for that item only, move on
- write a permission denial at the top of this run's report
- two failures in a row on one item: stop, "needs your action"
## Logs
- copy times from tool output, not from memory

Our values: lane 1 is two posts a day and three days per site, lane 3 holds ad status changes and publish clicks a permission check refused, and lane 4 holds proposals to cut channels.

What is left

Session jobs have to be registered again every seven days. The next number to count is how many days a "needs your decision" item waits before it is decided; the log already has a four-day case. If that number does not drop, the fix is to change when the report gets read, not to shrink the person's lane.

Questions, consulting or collaboration

Email us with a question about this note, consulting on app development or on adopting AI agents such as Claude Code, or a collaboration idea.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com · Subscribe via RSS

Giving an agent rules and limits: all 5 parts

  1. What survives Claude Code auto-compaction: the summary, recent files and the memory index
  2. Keeping secrets away from an AI coding agent: one rule for chat, logs and token permissions

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Claude Code scheduled job last?

The session jobs used here expire after seven days and stop as soon as the session ends, so the rules file carries a renewal date and the jobs are registered again before they lapse.

Why is the agent's click blocked after a person approved it?

The tool's permission classifier judges each click on its own, apart from any approval in the chat. That is why clicks that spend money sit in the person's lane from the start.

What should an AI agent ask about before acting?

Five things: a channel tried for the first time, work on weak evidence, anything publicly visible, anything hard to undo, and anything touching money, accounts or policy. "Anything that costs money" alone was not enough, because in one case the cost only showed up at the last step.

Sources: the operating rules file and posting log (October 9 to 22, 2026), daily reports, agent memory files and the Claude Code session transcript. Times are Korea Standard Time.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Android blank Hangul: 8,693 empty glyphs in cmap – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Android showed some Hangul as blank gaps: NanumSquare's cmap claimed 11,172 syllables but drew only 2,479

When a font's cmap says it has a character it cannot draw, Android uses that font anyway and paints a blank instead of falling back to the system font. Removing the empty entries from the cmap fixed it.

On the night of 2026-09-15, the operator of our Korean spelling checker, SugarSpeller, noticed that the rare syllable 밣 showed up in the input box but turned into an empty gap inside the chat bubble. The cause was the bundled NanumSquare Light font. Its cmap (the table that maps character codes to glyph numbers) listed all 11,172 precomposed Hangul syllables, yet 8,693 of those glyphs had zero bytes of outline data. We removed 13,948 outline-less entries from the cmap, and the fix shipped in version 1.6.017.

Sources: the fix commit, the 1.6.017 changelog entry and the work log in the app repository. Numbers were re-measured on 2026-10-22 from the font files before and after the fix.

The glyph for 밣 had 0 bytes and a width of 910

Android's text layout engine, Minikin, picks the font for each character by reading the cmap. It never checks whether the outline is empty. Following 밣 (U+BC23) through the file gives a four-step chain.

  1. The cmap maps U+BC23 to glyph 12552.
  2. The loca table (where each glyph's data starts and ends) gives glyph 12552 a length of 0.
  3. The hmtx table still gives it an advance width of 910, the same as a normal syllable such as 받. So the reader sees a one-character gap, not a tofu box. All 8,693 empty syllables had width 910.
  4. Since the app font already answered yes, no fallback to the system font happens.

Once the entry is out of the cmap, the app font says no and Android finds the character in the system font. The cmap went from 17,559 entries to 3,611.

Re-measured: only 2,479 syllables had outlines

These values come from reading the tables directly with Python's struct module, without fontTools.

ItemBeforeAfter
Hangul syllables in the cmap11,1722,479
Of those, 0-byte outlines8,6930
Visible characters with no outline (spaces and controls excluded)13,9480
Characters with outlines3,5753,575
Glyph count18,15518,155
File size (bytes)750,932715,448

The 13,948 split into 8,693 Hangul syllables, 4,890 Han characters (hanja) and 365 others, including the bullet • and several arrows. Not a single hanja could be drawn by this font. The 2,479 surviving syllables are all 2,350 syllables of KS X 1001, the legacy Korean character set that covers everyday text, plus 129 more. Those 129 include 뷁, which is outside KS X 1001. A test that used 뷁 as its "rare syllable" would have passed.

Only the chat bubble broke because it was a TextView

The symptom as first described: visible in the input box, blank in the bubble, fine on the Classic screen. The app theme applied this font to every TextView through android:textViewStyle, and the bubble was a TextView. The input box and the Classic result box were EditTexts. According to the commit, AppCompat's EditText does not pick up the theme's android:editTextStyle, so they used the system font. The Classic screen survived by accident. Every TextView in the app was affected.

The agent's first check said 밣 was there

An AI coding agent found the cause, but its first measurement pointed the wrong way. It only checked whether 밣 was in each font's cmap: NanumSquare said yes, and the Gamja Flower subset used for greeting cards said no. What turned it around was file size. A font with 17,559 cmap entries in 750 KB looked too small to hold every syllable, so the agent measured outline lengths. The 8,693 figure came out 1 minute 35 seconds after the problem was raised.

The first trial fix was wrong too. It removed 13,991 entries without filtering, including 32 control characters and 3 space characters that are supposed to be empty. Right after the operator approved the plan, the agent re-filtered by Unicode category before applying it, and the final count became 13,948.

The third mistake was caught by a person. After committing, the agent said it could not check rendering on a device and handed the visual check to the operator, even though it had booted an Android 14 emulator in software mode the day before in the same session. The operator asked for a deep review and cross-check before release, and granted the KVM permission the agent asked for. At 08:37 the next morning, an Android 14 emulator showed both 밣받다 and • fully drawn.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The font was probably shipped this way

The commit message guessed that "a subsetting tool removed the glyphs but kept the cmap". While writing this note we ran the same measurement on the NanumSquare files the site uses to draw figures. NanumSquare ExtraBold matched the app's file exactly: 8,693 empty syllables, 13,948 visible characters without outlines. NanumSquare Regular had 8,822 empty syllables (Figure 2).

The site's files are weights the app never had, so they are not copies. All three carry a 2016 "Version 1.000" build string, and the app's file was already in the repository's first commit on 2020-12-16. We have not compared them with the official download, so the commit's guess stays unconfirmed. For contrast, the properly cut Gamja Flower subset listed only 2,349 syllables in its cmap.

We trimmed the cmap instead of swapping fonts or adding a fallback chain

NanumGothic, already in the app at 4,691,820 bytes, draws all 11,172 syllables, but switching to it changes the look of the whole app. Replacing the file with a complete NanumSquare Light was estimated at about 4 MB more, and the measurements above make it unclear whether such a file exists. Outside the session we also considered a fallback chain with Typeface.CustomFallbackBuilder (API 29). It does not help, because the font for each character is still chosen by cmap.

Trimming the cmap keeps every glyph in place, so the result can be checked one to one against the original. The cost is that rare syllables and hanja appear in the system typeface. If you bundle a font in a Korean app, do not trust cmap coverage to tell you it "supports Hangul". Add a test that measures outline lengths.

When this check does not work

  • CFF-based OTF fonts have no loca table. The app's regression test treats the length as -1 there and passes silently.
  • Fonts with only a format 12 cmap: the test reads format 4 only and passes on an empty map.
  • Characters the system font also lacks still show tofu after the trim.
  • Screens where every character must share one typeface need a different font.

We checked View-based TextViews on one Android 14 emulator. We did not check Compose Text.

How to check the fonts in your own app

  1. List every font in res/font and assets.
  2. For each font, read glyph numbers from the cmap and lengths from loca, and count entries with length 0. Skip Unicode categories Cc, Cf, Zs, Zl, Zp and the three Hangul fillers (U+115F, U+1160, U+3164).
  3. Compare the number of drawable syllables with the 2,350 of KS X 1001.
  4. Pick on-screen test characters from the step 2 output.

Step 2 takes the 24 lines below. On the original file it prints blank 13948 / hangul 11172, drawn 2479. On a CFF-based OTF font it stops with KeyError: 'loca', because there is no loca table, and on a font without a format 4 subtable it prints hangul 0 (checked on 2026-10-23 with Noto Sans KR OTF and with a copy whose format 4 subtables were relabeled). If you see hangul 0, check the subtable formats first.

import struct, sys, unicodedata
d = open(sys.argv[1], "rb").read()
u16 = lambda p: struct.unpack_from(">H", d, p)[0]
u32 = lambda p: struct.unpack_from(">I", d, p)[0]
T = {d[12+16*i:16+16*i].decode("latin1"): u32(20+16*i) for i in range(u16(4))}
def glyph_len(g):                      # loca: short(0) / long(1)
    lo = T["loca"]
    if u16(T["head"] + 50): return u32(lo+4*g+4) - u32(lo+4*g)
    return 2 * (u16(lo+2*g+2) - u16(lo+2*g))
cmap = {}
for i in range(u16(T["cmap"] + 2)):    # format 4 subtables only
    s = T["cmap"] + u32(T["cmap"] + 8 + 8*i)
    if u16(s) != 4: continue
    n = u16(s + 6); e = s + 14; st = e + n + 2; de = st + n; ro = de + n
    for k in range(0, n, 2):
        a, b, dl, r = u16(st+k), u16(e+k), struct.unpack_from(">h", d, de+k)[0], u16(ro+k)
        for c in range(a, min(b, 0xFFFE) + 1):
            g = (c + dl) & 0xFFFF if r == 0 else u16(ro + k + r + 2*(c - a))
            if r and g: g = (g + dl) & 0xFFFF
            if g: cmap[c] = g
ok = lambda c: c in (0x115F, 0x1160, 0x3164) or unicodedata.category(chr(c)) in ("Cc", "Cf", "Zs", "Zl", "Zp")
blank = [c for c, g in cmap.items() if glyph_len(g) == 0 and not ok(c)]
han = [c for c in cmap if 0xAC00 <= c <= 0xD7A3]
print(f"blank {len(blank)} / hangul {len(han)}, drawn {sum(glyph_len(cmap[c]) > 0 for c in han)}")

The cleanup itself was a fontTools script added in the fix commit. With fontTools it deletes, in every cmap subtable, the entries that point to outline-less glyphs, and keeps the characters skipped in step 2. It refuses fonts without a glyf table.

font = TTFont(src)
glyf = font["glyf"]
for table in font["cmap"].tables:
    cmap = getattr(table, "cmap", None) or {}
    for cp, name in list(cmap.items()):
        if glyf[name].numberOfContours == 0 and not is_blank_ok(cp):
            del cmap[cp]
font.save(dst)
  1. After trimming, confirm every removed entry was empty and the count of characters with outlines is unchanged (3,575 here).
  2. Put the original font back and make sure the test fails, as in Catch fake AI-written tests by deleting their guards.
  3. Check that base/res/font in the release AAB holds the fixed file.

What is left

The site's figure and share-image tools use those same NanumSquare files, so any syllable outside KS X 1001 would come out blank in a figure (the second cell of the first figure), so this note keeps 밣 out of its title. Swapping the figure font and teaching the app's test about CFF and format 12 are still open.

Questions, consulting or collaboration

Email us with a question about this note, consulting on app development or on adopting AI agents such as Claude Code, or a collaboration idea.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com · Subscribe via RSS

FAQ

Why do some Korean characters show as blank spaces in my Android app?

Most likely your bundled font lists them in its cmap but has empty outlines for them. Measuring the outline length behind each cmap entry shows it at once.

How do I tell a tofu box (□) from a blank gap?

A tofu box means no font, fallbacks included, has the character. A gap one character wide means the cmap lists it but the outline is empty. Every empty syllable in this font had width 910.

Which characters should I use to test a Korean font?

Ones the font actually cannot draw, found by inspecting it. This font drew 뷁 but not 밣.

item.title: Korean line breaks in Compose and stacked labels – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · How-to

Jetpack Compose splits Korean between syllables, but the stacked 'R/u/l/e' label came from how a Row measures

Jetpack Compose breaks Korean words between syllables. A shared WordBreak.Phrase style and a longest-word width check fixed it; the vertically stacked labels had a separate cause.

In a row that puts a label next to its value, the word "Rule" was standing on its end: R, u, l, e, one letter per line. We saw it on September 25, 2026, during a real-device pass of three photo apps on a Galaxy S21 (Android 15), and the same shape turned up in "Versio/n", "1.0.1-debu/g" and the Korean "오른쪽으/로" ("to the right", split before its last syllable). They looked alike but had two causes. The first three came from a Row that measured the value first and left the label almost no width. The Korean one came from Compose treating every Hangul syllable boundary as a break point. Both were fixed, separately, in one design-system module the three apps share.

Sources: the fix commit and same-day changelog in the app repository, the HWP Viewer SugarDoc device test report (2026-10-06) and the Android Developers reference, as of October 21, 2026.

Five broken spots, all inside shared components

Every defect sat in a shared component. The September 25 QA was run by four AI coding agents in turn: one per app, then a fourth that reproduced every finding with its own screenshots and read the code behind each root cause. The table copies the symptoms recorded that day in the CHANGELOG and in code comments.

SymptomComponentCauseFix
"R/u/l/e", "Versio/n", "1.0.1-debu/g"Label/value rows, settings rowsRow measured the value first and gave the label what was leftPairLayout: side by side if both fit, otherwise the value drops below
"오른쪽으/로", "Transparen/t PNG"Option tile grid, action buttonsA word wider than its cell; Compose reported one Hangul syllable as the minimum widthMeasure the longest word and fall back to one column
"Quick compress" did not fit a third of the widthSegmented controlLarge fontStacked tiles from 150% font scale
"Web" and "Custom" hidden off-screenChoice chip rowHorizontal scrollingFlowRow wrapping
Korean words such as "메일" (mail) could split at 200% fontEvery text styleSyllable boundaries counted as break pointsWordBreak.Phrase

The three apps are Compress Image, Flip & Rotate Image and Convert Image JPG PNG WEBP, and all of them depend on the same design-system module. The fix commit touched 57 files, but the line-breaking work is concentrated in a handful of files in that module.

Compose treats Hangul syllable boundaries as break points

LineBreak.WordBreak decides where Compose may split a word. The LineBreak.WordBreak reference describes Default as the locale's default word-breaking rules: Latin scripts break between words, while languages that don't use whitespace (the page's example is Japanese) can break between characters. Phrase does not insert breaks between characters of the same phrase unit and is "ideal for short text such as titles and UI labels". Both values were added in Compose 1.3.0.

Korean does put spaces between words, yet the apps still split inside them. A comment in the repository's WordWidth.kt records why: Compose's own minimum intrinsic width treats every Hangul syllable as a break point. So the grid believed "오른쪽으로" fitted in the width of a single syllable, kept two columns and cut the word in the middle.

The platform adds its own limit. Per the LineBreakConfig reference, phrase-based breaking (LINE_BREAK_WORD_STYLE_PHRASE) arrived in API level 33 (Android 13), its support depends on the locale, and it has no effect where the locale is unsupported. These apps have minSdk 29, which means Phrase does nothing on Android 10 to 12.

WordBreak.Phrase lives in one shared TextStyle

A single style() function in SugarType.kt builds every step of the type scale, so it is the only place that sets lineBreak. No screen code changed.

private val WordAwareBreak =
    LineBreak.Simple.copy(wordBreak = LineBreak.WordBreak.Phrase)
private fun style(weight: FontWeight, size: Int, line: Int, spacing: Boolean = false) = TextStyle(
    // fontFamily, fontSize, lineHeight, letterSpacing ...
    lineBreak = WordAwareBreak,
)

If your Compose app has Korean screens, set Phrase once in the shared TextStyle and do not add it to individual Text calls. Per-screen settings get forgotten the next time someone adds a screen. The same comment says a word wider than the line still breaks. (The Korean hero titles also got zero-width break points after the "·" separator.)

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The longest word decides how many columns fit

The option tile grid picks its column count from the minimum intrinsic width each tile reports. For Korean that number is one syllable wide, so the module gained a function that measures whole words: split on whitespace, measure each word on one line, return the widest.

text.split(Regex("\\s+")).filter { it.isNotEmpty() }.maxOfOrNull { word ->
    measurer.measure(word, style, softWrap = false, maxLines = 1).size.width
} ?: 0

Tile titles and subtitles report that value as their minimum intrinsic width (minIntrinsicWidthAtLeast, a small LayoutModifier), and the grid compares it with the cell width.

val cols = when {
    requested == 1 -> 1
    largeFont -> 1
    measurables.any { it.minIntrinsicWidth(Constraints.Infinity) > cellWidthFor(requested) } -> 1
    else -> requested
}

In app code, Flip & Rotate Image's four action buttons use the same function. When the longest word of any label is wider than half the screen minus the button chrome, the buttons go one per row instead of two.

From 150% font scale, stack; for chips, use FlowRow

One constant defines "large font": LARGE_FONT_SCALE = 1.5f in Chips.kt. At or above it, three components switch to a vertical layout.

  • Segmented control: the segments become option tiles stacked top to bottom. The check icon went too; it was taking a third of a segment's width.
  • Option tile grid: one column, whatever was requested.
  • Flip & Rotate Image's action buttons: one per row.

The choice chip row used to be a Row with horizontalScroll. Chips past the edge simply hid there, and nothing told the user that "Web" or "Custom" existed. With FlowRow they wrap onto the next line.

// before: Row(modifier = modifier.horizontalScroll(rememberScrollState()), ...)
FlowRow(
    modifier = modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(SugarSpacing.sm),
) { /* FilterChip ... */ }

A Row from four days earlier, and a button width that missed by 2 px

"R/u/l/e" had nothing to do with Korean. The label/value row came from the design v2 commit (2026-09-21), written together with an AI coding agent. It was a Row with Modifier.weight(1f, fill = false) on the label and no weight on the value. A Row measures unweighted children first, so a long value took the whole width and the label folded into the few pixels left, one letter per line.

Four days later, the cross-check agent in the device QA flagged this structure while reading the code behind the finding. The new PairLayout measures each slot's natural width (maxIntrinsicWidth) first. If the sum fits the line, they sit side by side; if not, the value moves under the label.

The second mistake was a number. The action-button chrome adds up to exactly 76 dp: 24 dp of OutlinedButton padding on each side, a 20 dp icon and an 8 dp gap. According to the code comment, at 130% font "오른쪽으로" measured 2 px under the space that exact figure left, and it still wrapped. The value was fixed at BUTTON_CHROME = 84.dp, the exact chrome plus 8 dp of slack.

The same defect came back by another route. In the HWP Viewer SugarDoc device test on 2026-10-06, the format placeholder split into "HW/PX" (S21) and "HW/P" (S20) at 200% font. That app uses the same design-system module, so Phrase was already on, but "HWPX" is a single word and a word wider than its box still breaks. Pinning the placeholder to one line and letting it shrink to fit fixed that, but "HWP 3.0" did not fit even at the smallest step and got clipped to "HWP 3.(" instead. The final fix shortened placeholder names to four characters or fewer ("HWP3"), while the badge and the TalkBack label keep "HWP 3.0".

Checklist

After the September 25 fixes, a separate agent checked every fix on the device and a person checked again by hand, across 1.0/1.3/2.0 font scale, Korean and English, light and dark, and landscape, with no regressions. The list below is drawn from these fixes.

  • The shared TextStyle sets lineBreak = LineBreak.Simple.copy(wordBreak = LineBreak.WordBreak.Phrase). Android 12 and lower ignore it, so the items below still matter.
  • Layouts that choose a column count look at the longest word, not Compose's minimum intrinsic width.
  • At fontScale 1.5 and above, segmented controls, grids and button rows switch to a vertical layout.
  • No option hides behind horizontal scrolling (FlowRow).
  • Label/value rows are not left to Row weights.
  • Computed padding includes the error seen on a device (8 dp this time).
  • Single-word short labels, such as format names like "HWPX", fit their box at 200% font.

One item is still open: on the input screen of Convert Image JPG PNG WEBP, the size badge wraps as "JPEG · 1.3 / MB", recorded as a cosmetic leftover in the 2026-09-25 CHANGELOG entry. The full pre-release check list is in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app.

Questions, consulting or collaboration

Email us with a question about this note, consulting on app development or on adopting AI agents such as Claude Code, or a collaboration idea.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com · Subscribe via RSS

FAQ

How do I make Jetpack Compose wrap Korean by word instead of by syllable?

Set lineBreak = LineBreak.Simple.copy(wordBreak = LineBreak.WordBreak.Phrase) in your TextStyle. Put it in the shared typography once and every Text picks it up. Android 12 and lower ignore it, so keep a layout check based on the longest word as well.

Why does a word still split in the middle with WordBreak.Phrase?

Phrase still breaks a word that is wider than its line or cell. Widen the cell, use fewer columns or shorten the text. HWP Viewer SugarDoc saw the 'HWPX' placeholder split into 'HW/PX' at 200% font, pinned it to one line with auto-shrink, and shortened 'HWP 3.0', which still did not fit, to 'HWP3'.

Which font scales should a Compose layout be tested at?

These apps were checked at 1.0, 1.3 and 2.0 font scale, combined with Korean and English, light and dark, and landscape. Their layouts switch to vertical at 1.5, so test on both sides of that switch.
